meta.blurb: At nine o'clock Grace holds an empty mug in her quiet kitchen. After a lifetime of teaching, she has nowhere to be. Kofi works nights and loses his free hours to his phone. Both find small, real reasons to start the day.
meta.bible: Grace: a retired teacher aged sixty-eight, who taught for forty years, lives alone on Alder Road and finds her days empty. Her daughter Ruth lives far away and calls on Sundays; Ruth's son Theo is six. Kofi: a man of twenty-four who works nights at the Eastgate warehouse and spends his free hours on his phone. His sister Abena lives in another part of town; his gran taught him to cook groundnut stew. Ms Okoro is Kofi's manager. Yaw is Kofi's friend, who plays football on Saturdays at the Marsh Lane pitch. Dev: Grace's neighbour on Alder Road, who grows tomatoes; his sister's small dog is called Biscuit. Mae works at the Hill Road library. Ines leads the Tuesday walking group. Key terms: Reasons, Curiosity, Routine, Commitment, Gentle goals. The book speaks to You in kind, practical, everyday words. It gives general encouragement only and says when to talk to a doctor. Voice: warm, simple, concrete and quietly humorous. No invented studies, numbers or quotes. A reason to get up does not have to be a grand purpose.
chapters: Things That Grow and Need You

beats.scene: An alarm clock rings on a bedside table in grey morning light
beats.summary: The alarm gets you out of bed, but a reason to get up is something else.

beats.scene: A hand reaches out and presses the snooze button again
beats.summary: Many of us press snooze, because the bed is warm and the day has not yet given us a reason.

beats.scene: A person sits on the edge of a bed, head bowed
beats.summary: Some mornings are heavy for nearly everyone, and that is normal.

beats.scene: Tired people wait at a bus stop in the early morning dark
beats.summary: Almost everyone has felt this heaviness, so you are not alone with it.

beats.scene: A boat pushed from behind by a hand, pulled by a rope
beats.summary: An alarm pushes you out of bed, while a reason pulls you towards the day.

beats.scene: A child leaps out of bed on a bright holiday morning
beats.summary: As a child you probably jumped up on days when something good was waiting.

beats.scene: A heavy bag on the ground beside a kite lifting into the wind
beats.summary: A duty weighs on you like a bag, while a reason can lift you like a kite.

beats.scene: A small notebook and a pen lie open on a kitchen table
beats.summary: This book asks you to try small experiments, and a notebook will help you keep track.

beats.scene: A winding path crosses green hills towards one small house
beats.summary: A reason does not have to be a grand purpose; it only has to be enough for today.

beats.scene: A person opens a window on a quiet morning and breathes in
beats.summary: Your first task is to notice, tomorrow morning, how you feel before you get up.

beats.scene: Grace stands in her quiet kitchen holding an empty mug at nine o'clock
beats.summary: Grace has retired after forty years of teaching, and at nine o'clock her kitchen is silent.

beats.scene: A school bell hangs in a corridor of children in uniform
beats.summary: Grace still hears the school bell in her head, though it stopped ringing for her months ago.

beats.scene: An empty wall calendar with every square blank
beats.summary: Her calendar is blank for the first time in decades, and she does not know what to do with that.

beats.scene: Grace sits in an armchair watching the clock above a silent television
beats.summary: The mornings stretch so long that Grace starts to watch the clock.

beats.scene: A silent telephone sits beside a framed snapshot of a young woman and boy
beats.summary: Her daughter Ruth lives far away and calls on Sundays, so the rest of the week is quiet.

beats.scene: A red marking pen lies on a desk beside an unopened pile of paper
beats.summary: Grace misses being useful, and she misses being asked.

beats.scene: Grace walks slowly along a shopping street carrying one small bag
beats.summary: She makes her errands last longer to fill the time, and it does not feel good.

beats.scene: Grace washes a cup at the sink and talks to the radio
beats.summary: She notices that she has begun to talk to the radio, and it makes her smile and worry.

beats.scene: Grace sits on her bed at night with the lamp off, thinking
beats.summary: At night she asks herself an honest question: what is there to get up for?

beats.scene: Grace writes a question at the top of a new notebook's first page
beats.summary: She buys a notebook and writes the question at the top; it is the first thing she has planned in months.

beats.scene: Kofi in a bright vest pushes a trolley through a warehouse at night
beats.summary: Kofi, twenty-four, works nights at the Eastgate warehouse, moving boxes while the city sleeps.

beats.scene: Kofi rides a bus home through grey dawn, his head against the window
beats.summary: He rides home at dawn while everyone else rides to work, and he feels a step out of time.

beats.scene: Kofi eats cereal at a small table as daylight spreads across the kitchen
beats.summary: He eats breakfast at seven, just as his own day is ending.

beats.scene: Kofi lies in bed at noon while his phone glows in his hand
beats.summary: After sleeping, Kofi lies in bed and scrolls, and the hours disappear.

beats.scene: A phone screen shows endless short videos in a dim room
beats.summary: He watches things he does not even enjoy, because it is easier than choosing something.

beats.scene: A kitchen with unwashed plates as the light fades in the window
beats.summary: By five o'clock the daylight is going and he has done nothing, which leaves him feeling heavy.

beats.scene: A phone shows a sent message with no reply beside cold tea
beats.summary: His friends work in the daytime, so replies come slowly and the gaps feel big.

beats.scene: Kofi on a video call with his sister Abena, who is laughing
beats.summary: His sister Abena asks what he did today, and he has no answer.

beats.scene: Kofi stands in the locker room looking at the clock before a shift
beats.summary: He does not hate his job, but the only things he looks forward to are payday and sleep.

beats.scene: Kofi sticks a yellow note with a question on his fridge door
beats.summary: After Abena's call, he writes a question on a note and sticks it on his fridge: what am I looking forward to?

beats.scene: A steaming cup of coffee and a watering can beside a sunny window
beats.summary: A reason can be tiny, such as a coffee, a plant or someone waiting.

beats.scene: A short wall of bricks rises row by row in a sunny garden
beats.summary: Many small reasons can add up, like bricks, to a day worth starting.

beats.scene: A person counts three small things on their fingers beside a window
beats.summary: Try to have three small reasons each day, so that no single one has to carry everything.

beats.scene: A climber looks up at a distant peak, then down at the next step
beats.summary: Big purposes can feel too far away, while a small reason is near enough to reach tomorrow.

beats.scene: Two friends at a café table, one holding out a small wrapped gift
beats.summary: Someone waiting for you counts as a reason, even if it is only for a chat over tea.

beats.scene: A warm bread roll with butter on a plate by a sunny window
beats.summary: Looking forward to a good breakfast is a respectable reason, and nobody needs to be impressed by it.

beats.scene: A thick novel with a bookmark halfway through lies on a pillow
beats.summary: A story you are halfway through gives you a reason to find out what happens next.

beats.scene: Small smooth stones balanced in a stack on a beach
beats.summary: Small pleasures do not have to be productive, they only have to be yours.

beats.scene: Grace writes the first line in her notebook at the kitchen table
beats.summary: Grace writes her first honest answer: the library opens at ten, and she likes the smell of books.

beats.scene: Kofi writes on a yellow note, beside a loaf of fresh bread
beats.summary: Kofi's first answer is the bakery on his corner, where the first hot loaves come out as he passes.

beats.scene: A person writes a numbered list in a notebook at a sunny breakfast table
beats.summary: Look back over the last year and list five things you really looked forward to.

beats.scene: A shoebox of old snapshots is spread across a bed
beats.summary: Old photos and messages can remind you of days you enjoyed more than you remembered.

beats.scene: A girl rides a bicycle down a hill with her arms wide
beats.summary: Remember what you loved at ten years old, because some of it may still be waiting.

beats.scene: A man absorbed in his work as sunlight moves across the wall behind him
beats.summary: Notice which activities make time pass without you noticing.

beats.scene: Grace draws a diagram on a whiteboard while pupils lean forward
beats.summary: Grace's list is full of teaching moments, such as the pupil who finally understood fractions.

beats.scene: Kofi's list on the back of an envelope lies beside a mug
beats.summary: Kofi's list is shorter, but it holds football, his gran's cooking and a good song.

beats.scene: Two lists lie side by side with the same word circled on each
beats.summary: Look for patterns in your list, such as people, making things, movement or learning.

beats.scene: A person crosses a line off a list with a small frown
beats.summary: Some old reasons are gone, and it is fine to be sad about them before looking for new ones.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass rests over one warm line on a handwritten list
beats.summary: Pick the one item that still feels warm, and ask how a small piece of it could fit into this week.

beats.scene: Grace and Kofi each circle one item on their own lists, in different kitchens
beats.summary: Grace circles finding things out and Kofi circles cooking, and each plans one small first step.

beats.scene: A child and an older woman look through a magnifying glass at a leaf
beats.summary: Curiosity is fuel, and one new question a day gives the mind somewhere to go.

beats.scene: A jar of folded paper slips sits on a kitchen shelf
beats.summary: Write your questions on slips of paper and keep them in a jar, to be answered one at a time.

beats.scene: Grace watches a small brown bird on the garden fence through binoculars
beats.summary: Grace becomes curious about a small brown bird in her garden and wants to know its name.

beats.scene: Grace and Mae at the library desk look through a shelf of bird books
beats.summary: At the library Mae helps Grace find a bird guide, and Grace is surprised how glad she is to be helped.

beats.scene: Grace sits at the window with a bird book open and a pencil
beats.summary: Learning something new is rewarding because you can feel yourself improving.

beats.scene: Grace points at a small plain bird in the garden and smiles
beats.summary: After a week, Grace names her mystery visitor: a dunnock, a quiet brown bird that likes hedges.

beats.scene: Kofi chats with the baker behind a counter of loaves
beats.summary: Kofi asks the baker why the bread tastes so good, and the answer is a long, slow rise.

beats.scene: A person follows one question across a laptop with a cup of tea
beats.summary: Following a question for a while, with no deadline, is a kind of play for the mind.

beats.scene: Two neighbours talk over a garden fence while one points at a plant
beats.summary: Ask people questions, because most people are pleased to be asked about what they know.

beats.scene: A notebook page shows three crossed-out questions and one new one
beats.summary: Each answer tends to bring a new question, and that chain is a rope pulling you into tomorrow.

beats.scene: Kofi tastes a red stew from a wooden spoon in a small kitchen
beats.summary: Kofi decides to cook one new dish each week, and he starts looking forward to Sundays.

beats.scene: A stained handwritten recipe card lies beside a pot of groundnut stew
beats.summary: Kofi finds his gran's old recipe for groundnut stew and decides to cook it first.

beats.scene: Kofi chops onions and tomatoes on a board with a sharp knife
beats.summary: The simple steps of chopping, stirring and tasting keep his mind in one place.

beats.scene: Kofi holds up a steaming bowl to a video call with his sister
beats.summary: Cooking for someone else makes it even better, and Abena asks for the recipe.

beats.scene: A woman kneads dough with floury hands at a wooden table
beats.summary: Using your hands, whether in cooking, gardening or mending, brings a calm satisfaction.

beats.scene: Grace sews a torn cushion cover with a needle and thread
beats.summary: Grace mends a torn cushion cover, and the repair is the first thing she has finished in weeks.

beats.scene: A row of finished jars of jam stands on a kitchen shelf
beats.summary: Finished things are visible, and being able to point at what you made feels different from endless tasks.

beats.scene: A wooden stool being sanded smooth in a garden shed
beats.summary: Grace's neighbour Dev gives her an old stool to sand and paint, and shows her how to start.

beats.scene: A clock shows that hours have passed while hands are busy at a table
beats.summary: Busy hands quiet a busy mind, which is why many people find repetitive crafts soothing.

beats.scene: A table holds stew, a loaf of bread and a mended cushion
beats.summary: A week of making things adds up, so write down one thing your hands made.

beats.scene: A small plate with a biscuit is placed beside a kettle ready for morning
beats.summary: Prepare a small treat the night before, so that the morning has something to offer.

beats.scene: A cup, spoon and tea bag are laid on a tray by the kettle
beats.summary: Setting things out at night removes small decisions from a tired morning.

beats.scene: A pleasant morning corner with a favourite chair, a plant and a radio playing
beats.summary: A morning routine you enjoy makes it easier to begin.

beats.scene: A person sits with both hands around a warm mug, looking at a garden
beats.summary: Give the first ten minutes of the day to something slow and pleasant, with no hurry.

beats.scene: Grace arranges a blanket on her chair and a bird book beside the window
beats.summary: Grace builds her morning corner, and for the first time in months she hurries to the kitchen.

beats.scene: Sunlight falls across a rumpled bed and a clock showing three in the afternoon
beats.summary: Kofi's morning begins in the afternoon, and the same idea works at any hour.

beats.scene: A warm slice of bread with butter sits on a plate in the sun
beats.summary: Kofi adds a warm slice of bakery bread with butter to his wake-up, and it makes him sit up.

beats.scene: A person writes three short lines in a notebook by a bedside lamp
beats.summary: Each evening, name one thing to look forward to tomorrow, and write it down.

beats.scene: Two mornings side by side, one rushed and untidy, the other calm and bright
beats.summary: A calm routine is not a strict one; it is made of small habits you like.

beats.scene: A young tree bends in the wind beside a cracked wooden post
beats.summary: A routine should bend rather than break, and it must be gentle enough to forgive a bad day.

beats.scene: A woman opens heavy curtains and sunshine floods across a bedroom floor
beats.summary: Open the curtains and step outside, because daylight helps you wake up.

beats.scene: Grace stands on her doorstep in a dressing gown, holding a mug in sunshine
beats.summary: Grace starts to drink her morning tea on the doorstep, and the street looks different at that hour.

beats.scene: A man in trainers walks quickly along a tree-lined street at dawn
beats.summary: A little movement each day often lifts the mood and gives you energy.

beats.scene: Kofi in a jacket walks along a tree-lined road past the bakery at dawn
beats.summary: Kofi gets off the bus one stop early to walk the last ten minutes, and he begins to enjoy it.

beats.scene: Kofi and Grace nod to each other on a quiet street at dawn
beats.summary: Each morning Kofi passes Grace on her doorstep, and soon they nod, then say good morning.

beats.scene: A short walking loop is marked on a small hand-drawn street map
beats.summary: You do not need a gym, because a walk to the end of the street and back is a fine start.

beats.scene: A phone is plugged in to charge across the room while a person sleeps
beats.summary: Going to bed at regular times, and putting your phone away, makes mornings easier.

beats.scene: A bedroom with a low lamp, drawn curtains and a folded blanket
beats.summary: A wind-down hour before bed, with softer light, tells your body that the day is over.

beats.scene: A bedroom with dark curtains and a note on the door asking for quiet
beats.summary: Kofi, who sleeps in the day, makes his room dark and quiet so that his sleep is real rest.

beats.scene: A bedside table with only a glass of water and a book
beats.summary: Keep the bedside simple: a book, a glass of water and no screen.

beats.scene: Grace reads a notice on a library board about a Tuesday walking group
beats.summary: Grace sees a notice for a Tuesday morning walking group and hesitates.

beats.scene: Grace stands at a park gate in sturdy shoes and a coat, looking nervous
beats.summary: Grace goes along the first week, feeling nervous, and says very little.

beats.scene: A woman pours tea from a flask at a bench on a country path
beats.summary: Ines, the leader, offers her tea at the halfway bench and learns her name.

beats.scene: A group in raincoats and umbrellas walks together along a wet path
beats.summary: By the third week the others ask where she is if she is late, and she feels missed.

beats.scene: Kofi runs after a football on a floodlit local pitch with his friends
beats.summary: Kofi's friend Yaw asks him to join a Saturday football game, and Kofi says yes before he can change his mind.

beats.scene: A kit bag packed and waiting beside the front door on Friday night
beats.summary: Kofi packs his bag on Friday night, so the decision is already made when Saturday comes.

beats.scene: A muddy man sits laughing on the grass after a football game
beats.summary: After the game Kofi is muddy, tired and happier than he has been all week.

beats.scene: Two friends write a time and place in a shared diary
beats.summary: A small promise to someone else keeps you going when your own wish is weak.

beats.scene: A person types a message into a phone: see you at ten
beats.summary: Make the promise specific, with a time, a place and a name.

beats.scene: A hand holds open a door of a community hall for someone arriving
beats.summary: When you do not feel like going, remember that going is usually easier than it seemed and often feels better afterwards.

beats.scene: Mae at the library desk hands Grace a children's storybook, smiling
beats.summary: Mae hears Grace's old teacher voice and asks her to read to the children at the library on Thursdays.

beats.scene: Grace reads aloud in an armchair to an empty room, using different voices
beats.summary: Grace practises the voices for the story, just as she once did in her classroom.

beats.scene: Small children sit in a circle on a carpet looking up at Grace
beats.summary: The children sit in a circle, and one boy asks a question that makes her laugh.

beats.scene: Grace walks home across a park with her back straight and her head up
beats.summary: She walks home taller than she walked there, because somebody wanted her.

beats.scene: A grandmother and a small boy share a bench, each holding a snack
beats.summary: Being needed and being loved are both good reasons, and you can have both.

beats.scene: A six-year-old's drawing shows a smiling woman with a very big book
beats.summary: Theo draws Grace as a teacher with an enormous book, and she pins it on her fridge.

beats.scene: Dev holds a ladder against a tall hedge while Grace passes up the shears
beats.summary: Dev asks for help with a high branch, and helping a neighbour gives Grace a small, solid reason for the day.

beats.scene: A woman carries a covered dish across a street to a neighbour's door
beats.summary: A small act of kindness, such as taking soup to a neighbour, brightens their day and your own.

beats.scene: A tired person sits at a desk piled with papers beside a stop sign
beats.summary: Being needed should not turn into being used up, so a good reason gives you energy and does not only take it.

beats.scene: Kofi and his sister Abena carry a sofa up a narrow flight of stairs
beats.summary: Kofi helps Abena move into a new flat on his day off, and he feels useful for the first time in months.

beats.scene: A weekly calendar with one cheerful event marked each week
beats.summary: A weekly event that you look forward to gives the whole week a shape.

beats.scene: A long flat road crosses an empty plain with one tall signpost far ahead
beats.summary: A week with no landmarks is like a flat plain where there is nothing to walk towards.

beats.scene: Grace's weekly chart on the fridge shows Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday marked
beats.summary: Grace draws her week on paper and sees that it now has three posts to tie it to.

beats.scene: Kofi's weekly chart shows Saturday football and Sunday cooking, with long gaps between
beats.summary: Kofi's week has football and Sunday cooking, but there are still long empty stretches.

beats.scene: A person draws a small circle in the empty middle of a week
beats.summary: Fill the longest empty gap in your week with one small thing, such as a call, a swim or a class.

beats.scene: Grace sits on the sofa on Wednesday, relaxed, looking at her chart
beats.summary: On Wednesday Grace is not lonely, because she is looking forward to Thursday.

beats.scene: Calm swimmers glide along the lanes of a bright pool in the morning
beats.summary: A regular class, such as a swim or a choir, brings a place to be and people who know you.

beats.scene: A phone shows a recurring Sunday video call with a small boy waving
beats.summary: Grace and Ruth agree a regular Sunday call, and Theo joins in with a drawing of the week.

beats.scene: A diary page crammed with appointments, a person sighing beside it
beats.summary: Do not overbook yourself, because two or three landmarks are enough.

beats.scene: A calendar with a single gentle blank day marked with one word, nothing
beats.summary: Keep one day a week free of plans, so that your landmarks do not become a pile of chores.

beats.scene: A short staircase with a very low first step and a person stepping up
beats.summary: Choose gentle goals so small that you cannot fail, and let them grow.

beats.scene: A person smiles at a kitchen table, ticking off a task on a list
beats.summary: Goals you can finish in a single day give you a feeling of achievement every evening.

beats.scene: A short handwritten list of three tiny jobs lies beside a teapot
beats.summary: Grace writes three tiny jobs each morning: water the plants, read ten pages and walk to the postbox.

beats.scene: Kofi writes a tiny job on a sticky note beside a sink of plates
beats.summary: Kofi's first tiny job is to wash the dishes before his shift, and it changes how his flat feels.

beats.scene: A pair of trainers sits by a front door, one tied and one untied
beats.summary: When you do not feel like starting, begin with the smallest part, such as putting on your shoes.

beats.scene: A kitchen timer is set to five minutes beside a pile of papers
beats.summary: Try the five-minute rule: promise yourself you can stop after five minutes, and often you will not want to.

beats.scene: A tall pile of laundry beside a single neatly folded shirt
beats.summary: Start with one small item, because one folded shirt breaks the huge feeling of a big job.

beats.scene: Stepping stones cross a green lawn towards a garden bench
beats.summary: Gentle goals grow by inches, so next week you can add a little to what you did this week.

beats.scene: A tick chart on a wall shows a gap, then new ticks
beats.summary: Missing a day is not failing, and the chain of ticks can start again tomorrow.

beats.scene: In two separate rooms, Grace and Kofi each look at a ticked list
beats.summary: In the evening both of them look at their ticks, and the day feels well spent.

beats.scene: A woman stares blankly out of a window on a wet afternoon
beats.summary: Boredom and having no purpose are different, and noticing which one you feel helps.

beats.scene: A bored child stares at a wall and then picks up a crayon
beats.summary: Boredom is uncomfortable, but it can be a door to new ideas.

beats.scene: Two weather symbols sit side by side, a grey cloud and a dark storm
beats.summary: Boredom says, I need something; emptiness says, nothing matters, and it helps to learn which is which.

beats.scene: A person sleeps on a sofa under a blanket, a book on their chest
beats.summary: Rest is not laziness, and sometimes tiredness is mistaken for a lack of reasons.

beats.scene: Kofi sleeps deeply in a dark room, a clock showing ten hours have passed
beats.summary: Kofi sleeps for ten hours one weekend, and he notices that his mood is better afterwards.

beats.scene: A pot of tea steams beside a rainy window
beats.summary: Slowing down and enjoying small pleasures, like a cup of tea, gives the day its taste.

beats.scene: A person watches the rain through a window, holding a warm mug
beats.summary: Doing nothing on purpose, without guilt, is quite different from scrolling without noticing.

beats.scene: Grace eats a ripe pear slowly at her kitchen table, eyes closed
beats.summary: Grace eats a pear slowly and discovers how much flavour she had been missing.

beats.scene: A hammock hangs between two trees in dappled afternoon light
beats.summary: Kofi sets aside Sunday afternoons for rest, and he stops feeling guilty about it.

beats.scene: A phone battery icon being charged beside a lit lamp
beats.summary: Rest charges the battery that reasons run on, so rest is part of the plan, not a break from it.

beats.scene: Two adults blow bubbles in a park while laughing out loud
beats.summary: Adults forget how to play, and doing something purely for fun gives energy back.

beats.scene: Friends sit around a table with a board game, laughing over cards
beats.summary: Playing with other people, with board games, cards or silly quizzes, is a cheerful reason to meet.

beats.scene: Grace holds a cheap box of watercolour paints in a shop
beats.summary: Grace buys a cheap set of watercolour paints because she wants to paint her birds.

beats.scene: A clumsy watercolour of a robin sits on a kitchen table beside a paintbrush
beats.summary: Grace paints her birds, and she enjoys them even though they are not very good.

beats.scene: A beginner's hand holds a pencil while a teacher's hand guides it
beats.summary: Being a beginner is fine, because everyone starts without skill.

beats.scene: Grace sits among beginners at an adult painting class, laughing at a smudge
beats.summary: Grace joins a Wednesday painting class for beginners and remembers what it feels like to be the pupil.

beats.scene: Kofi sits on his bed with a borrowed guitar and a printed chord chart
beats.summary: Kofi borrows Yaw's old guitar and learns one chord, which sounds terrible.

beats.scene: A shelf of wobbly clay pots in different sizes
beats.summary: Wobbly pots and bad chords are evidence of trying, and trying is the point.

beats.scene: A child's drawing of a wonky yellow sun is pinned to a refrigerator
beats.summary: Children do not mind being bad at things, and we can borrow that attitude.

beats.scene: Kofi plays three chords on a guitar and grins
beats.summary: After three weeks Kofi can play three chords and a tune he recognises.

beats.scene: Grace's neighbour Dev waters rows of tomato plants in pots at dusk
beats.summary: Dev grows tomatoes in pots and checks them every day, and a living thing that needs you gives a day its structure.

beats.scene: Dev shows Grace how to press a seed into a small pot of soil
beats.summary: Dev gives Grace a pot and a few seeds, and she plants them on her window sill.

beats.scene: A tiny green seedling pushes up through dark soil
beats.summary: A seedling gives a small surprise each day, and Grace wonders whether it has grown overnight.

beats.scene: Grace waters a window sill pot with a small can in the early light
beats.summary: Her morning now has a job that needs her, and Grace gets up a little sooner.

beats.scene: A window sill holds small pots of basil, mint and parsley in the sun
beats.summary: Herbs on a window sill are easy, even in a tiny flat, and you can taste the reward.

beats.scene: A small dog waits expectantly at the door with a lead in its mouth
beats.summary: An animal that depends on you can give a reason to get up, although it is not right for everyone.

beats.scene: Grace walks a small brown dog along a leafy lane on a lead
beats.summary: Dev's sister's dog, Biscuit, needs a Monday walk, and Grace happily volunteers.

beats.scene: A person at a table reads a leaflet about adopting a puppy, looking thoughtful
beats.summary: A pet is a big promise, and there are other ways to enjoy animals, such as walking a neighbour's dog.

beats.scene: A spider plant in a hanging pot sits in the window of a kitchen
beats.summary: Kofi brings home a spider plant that is hard to kill, and he likes the challenge of keeping it alive.

beats.scene: A tomato plant with its first red fruit shines in the sun
beats.summary: Dev and Grace share the first ripe tomato of the season, and caring for it has been worth it.

beats.scene: Kofi talks with his manager at a warehouse desk, pointing to a computer screen
beats.summary: Kofi asks his manager about learning to run the stock system, and his job begins to feel different.

beats.scene: Kofi sits at a screen with Ms Okoro beside him, learning the stock system
beats.summary: Ms Okoro agrees to teach Kofi the stock system on quiet nights, an hour at a time.

beats.scene: Kofi counts boxes on a high shelf with a clipboard and finds a mistake
beats.summary: Kofi finds a shelf that has been labelled wrongly, and the small win makes the whole night better.

beats.scene: A small blue badge that reads stock team is pinned to a work vest
beats.summary: Learning a skill at work gives a path, and Kofi begins to see where his job could lead.

beats.scene: A person looks at the same warehouse shelf from two different angles
beats.summary: You may not be able to change your job, but you can change how you relate to it by looking for what you can learn or improve.

beats.scene: An empty wallet lies turned out on a table beside a calculator
beats.summary: Money is a real worry, and nobody should pretend that it is not.

beats.scene: A sunset glows over a town as someone sits on a hilltop bench

B1B2: An alarm clock can wake you up, but it cannot make you want to get out of bed. That wish comes from having a reason, and this book is about finding one.
Most of us have pressed snooze more than once, because the bed is warm and the day has given us no reason to leave. Ten more minutes feels like a small gift, although it rarely feels like enough.
Some mornings feel heavy, as if the blankets were made of lead. This happens to nearly everyone, and it does not mean that you are weak or broken.
Look around a bus stop at seven in the morning and you will see a great many tired faces. Almost everyone has felt the heaviness that you sometimes feel, so you are not alone with it.
An alarm pushes you out of bed, while a reason pulls you towards the day. Imagine a boat that is shoved from behind or drawn forward by a rope, and ask which journey feels better.
When you were a child, you probably jumped out of bed on birthdays and on the first morning of a holiday. Nobody needed to push you, because something good was waiting on the other side of the door.
A duty is something you carry, like a heavy bag on your back. A reason is more like a kite, because it lifts you up and asks only that you hold the string.
This book will ask you to try small experiments, and you will need something to write in. A cheap notebook and a pen are enough, and you can keep them next to your bed.
People often think that a reason to get up has to be a grand purpose. It does not, because a reason only needs to be enough for today.
Your first task is a very small one: tomorrow morning, before you get out of bed, notice how you feel. You do not need to change anything yet, because noticing is where this journey begins.
Grace is sixty-eight, and she retired from teaching last spring after forty years. At nine o'clock on a Monday she stands in her quiet kitchen, holding an empty mug.
At nine o'clock, Grace still hears the school bell in her head, although she has not worked for months. Her body remembers a rhythm that her life no longer has.
For the first time in decades, Grace's calendar has nothing written on it. She had dreamed of this freedom for years, but now the white squares look more like a question than a gift.
The mornings have become so long that Grace has started to watch the clock. She tells herself that she is resting, but she knows that she is mostly waiting.
Grace's daughter Ruth lives in another city, and she calls every Sunday evening. The telephone is silent for the other six days, and Grace has begun to notice the silence.
Grace finds an old red marking pen in a drawer and holds it for a while. She does not miss the marking so much as being useful, and being asked.
Grace has started to make her errands last longer, walking slowly to the shops and back. She buys one small thing, and it takes an hour, and it does not feel like a good use of the day.
One morning Grace realises that she has been answering the radio presenter out loud. She laughs about it, although part of her knows what it means.
Late one night, Grace sits in the dark and asks herself an honest question. She does not ask what she ought to do, but what she actually has to get up for.
The next day Grace buys a notebook and writes her question at the top of the first page. It is the first thing she has planned in months, and she is rather proud of it.
Kofi is twenty-four, and he works nights at the Eastgate warehouse. While the rest of the city sleeps, he moves boxes from one shelf to another under bright lights.
Kofi rides the bus home at dawn, past people on their way to work. They are starting their day while he is ending his, and he feels a step out of time.
Kofi eats his cereal at seven in the morning, just as the sun comes into his kitchen. For him it is the end of the day, and for most other people it is the beginning.
After a few hours of sleep, Kofi wakes and reaches for his phone. He tells himself that he will look for five minutes, and then the afternoon quietly disappears.
Kofi watches video after video, although he does not really enjoy most of them. It is easier to let the screen choose than to decide what he actually wants to do.
By five in the afternoon the daylight is already fading, and Kofi has done nothing at all. He feels heavy and a little ashamed, and he does not quite know why.
Kofi's friends all work during the day, so their replies to his messages come slowly. By the time they are free, he is already on his way to the warehouse.
Kofi's sister Abena calls him on video and asks, cheerfully, what he did today. He opens his mouth to answer and realises that he does not have one.
Kofi does not hate his job, and his colleagues are decent people. The trouble is that the only things he looks forward to are payday and sleep.
After Abena's call, Kofi writes a question on a yellow note and sticks it on his fridge: what am I looking forward to? He does not know the answer yet, but the question is at least in front of him.
People often imagine that a reason to get up must be something big. In fact it can be a cup of good coffee, a plant that needs water or a friend who will be waiting.
A single brick is not much to look at, but a wall is made of nothing else. In the same way, a handful of small reasons can add up to a day that is worth starting.
Try to have about three small reasons for every day, so that no single one has to do all the work. If one of them falls through, the other two will still be there to hold you up.
A big purpose can feel as far away as a mountain peak, and just as hard to reach on a cold morning. A small reason is near enough to touch, and you can reach it by tomorrow.
Someone who is waiting for you is already a reason to get up. It does not matter if it is only for a chat over a cup of tea.
Looking forward to a really good breakfast is a respectable reason to get up. Nobody has to be impressed by it, because it is yours and it works.
A story that you are halfway through is a wonderful reason to get up, or at least a reason to get comfortable. You want to know what happens next, and wanting is the beginning of energy.
Small pleasures do not have to be useful, impressive or productive. They only have to be yours, and they only have to make the day feel a little more worth entering.
Under her question, Grace writes her first honest answer: the library opens at ten. She loves the smell of books, and the thought of it makes her stand up a little straighter.
Kofi's first answer is the bakery on his corner. When he walks past in the late afternoon, the first hot loaves are just coming out of the oven.
Look back over the past year and write down five things that you really looked forward to. They can be tiny, and they do not have to be things that sound impressive.
Old photographs and messages can remind you of days that you enjoyed much more than you remembered. Look through them slowly, and notice where you were smiling.
Think about what you loved when you were about ten years old. Some of those loves have never really gone away, and they are only waiting for you to notice them.
Think about the times when an hour passed without your noticing, because you were so absorbed in what you were doing. Those moments are a clue that the activity matters to you.
When Grace makes her list, almost every line is about teaching. She remembers the shy boy who finally understood fractions, and the look on his face still makes her smile.
Kofi's list is much shorter than Grace's, but every line on it is real. It includes football, his gran's cooking and the feeling of hearing a really good song.
Look at your list and ask what the items have in common. You may find a pattern, such as people, making things, moving your body or learning.
Some of the things on your list may be gone for good, perhaps because a job has ended or a friend has moved away. It is fine to feel sad about that before you look for something new.
Pick the one item on your list that still feels warm when you think about it. Then ask how a very small piece of it could fit into this week.
Grace circles the words “finding things out”, and Kofi circles “cooking”. Neither of them knows the other exists yet, but each plans a small first step for tomorrow.
Curiosity is a kind of fuel, because a question gives the mind somewhere to go. You only need one new question a day to get the engine started.
Write each question that crosses your mind on a small slip of paper and drop it into a jar. Whenever you have a spare quarter of an hour, pull one out and go looking for the answer.
One morning a small brown bird lands on Grace's fence, and she realises that she does not know what it is. It is a strange feeling for a woman who has spent her life knowing the answers.
At the library, Mae finds Grace a thick guide to garden birds and asks what she has seen. Grace is surprised by how glad she is to be on the other side of the desk, asking for help.
Learning something new is rewarding because you can feel yourself getting better at it. Each morning Grace recognises a little more, and she marks each new bird in the book with her pencil.
After a week of watching, Grace finds her mystery visitor in the book. It is a dunnock, a quiet brown bird that likes low bushes, and she says its name out loud twice.
Kofi is curious about why the bakery's bread tastes so much better than the bread in the supermarket. The baker tells him it is mostly time, because the dough is left to rise slowly for many hours.
Following one question wherever it leads, with no deadline and no exam, is a kind of play for the mind. You may start with a bird and end up reading about a different continent.
Do not be afraid to ask other people your questions. Most people are pleased to be asked about the things that they know and love.
Each answer you find tends to bring a new question with it. That chain is a rope, and it pulls you gently into tomorrow.
Kofi decides to cook one new dish every week. Before long he is looking forward to Sundays, and he cannot remember the last time he could say that.
At the bottom of a drawer, Kofi finds a recipe card in his gran's handwriting for groundnut stew. He decides to cook it first, even though he has never made it himself.
Chopping, stirring and tasting are simple steps, and each one keeps Kofi's mind in the room. For the first time in weeks, his thoughts are not jumping from one screen to the next.
Kofi shows the finished stew to Abena on a video call, and she says it looks just like Gran's. He feels a warm flush of pride, and she asks him to send her the recipe.
Using your hands, whether to cook, to garden or to mend, brings a calm kind of satisfaction. The mind rests while the fingers work, and at the end there is something real to look at.
Grace finds a torn cushion cover and mends it with a needle and thread. It takes one hour, and it is the first thing she has finished in weeks.
A made thing can be seen and touched, and you can point at it and say, “I did that.” That feels very different from the endless tasks of the day, which never seem to be finished.
Grace's neighbour Dev, who lives next door, gives her an old wooden stool and some sandpaper. He shows her how to sand along the grain, and then he leaves her to it.

Busy hands can quiet a busy mind, and that is why many people find repeated crafts, such as knitting or sanding, so soothing. You do not need to be good at it, because the rhythm does most of the work.
Make a note, in your notebook, of one thing that your hands made this week. It might be a meal, a mended shirt or a bunch of flowers in a jar.
Before you go to bed, set out a small treat for the morning, such as a biscuit beside the kettle. When you wake up, there is already something waiting for you.
Setting out your cup and tea bag the night before takes away small decisions. A tired mind finds even tiny choices hard, so make the first steps of the morning easy.
Make your first half hour of the day pleasant. Play some music you like, sit in your favourite chair and drink something warm, and the rest of the morning will feel lighter.
Give the first ten minutes of your day to something slow and pleasant. Nobody is rushing you, and nothing important will go wrong if you sit and look out of the window.
Grace puts a blanket on her armchair and places the bird book beside the window. The next morning, for the first time in months, she walks to the kitchen quickly.
Kofi's morning begins in the afternoon, after he has slept through the daylight. The same advice works for him, because a pleasant start matters whenever your day begins.
Kofi starts to buy a small loaf from the bakery, and he saves a slice with butter for when he wakes. It is a tiny pleasure, but it gets him out of bed faster than any alarm has ever done.
Each evening, name one thing that you are looking forward to tomorrow, and write it in your notebook. It does not have to be exciting, and it can be as plain as a bowl of soup.
A calm routine is not the same as a strict one. It is made of small habits that you actually like, and it should feel more like a comfortable path than a rulebook.
Rules that are too strict will break, and a good routine bends. It should be gentle enough to forgive a bad day, so that one missed morning does not end the whole plan.
Open the curtains as soon as you get up, and if you can, step outside for a minute. Daylight tells your body that the day has started, and it helps you to wake up.
Grace begins to drink her morning tea on the front step in her dressing gown. The street looks different at that hour, and she is surprised by how much is going on.
A little movement each day often lifts the mood and gives you more energy. It does not have to be sport, because a brisk walk is enough.
Kofi decides to get off the bus one stop early and walk the last ten minutes home. At first it feels like an effort, but by the end of the week he is looking forward to it.
Each morning Kofi walks past Grace on her doorstep. First they nod, and then they say good morning, and soon each of them looks out for the other.
You do not need a gym or special clothes to begin. A walk to the end of your street and back is a perfectly good start, and you can add a little more each week.
Going to bed at about the same time each night makes mornings easier. Charge your phone across the room, so that it cannot tempt you in the dark.
Try a wind-down hour before bed, with softer lights and nothing exciting to read or watch. It tells your body that the day is finished, and that it is safe to rest.
Kofi sleeps during the day, so he hangs thick curtains and puts a polite note on his door. His room is now dark and quiet, and he finds that his sleep is deeper.
Keep your bedside simple, with a book, a glass of water and no screen. It is much harder to scroll for an hour when there is nothing to scroll with.
On the library noticeboard, Grace sees an advertisement for a Tuesday walking group. All are welcome, it says, but she is not sure that she counts.
The following Tuesday, Grace puts on her sturdy shoes and goes to the park gate. She feels nervous and says very little, but she walks the whole way round.
At the halfway bench, the leader, Ines, pours Grace a cup of tea from a flask. She asks her name and remembers it, which is a small kindness that Grace notices.
By the third week, Grace is five minutes late one rainy Tuesday. The others ask where she is, and she realises with a rush of warmth that she would be missed.
Kofi's friend Yaw asks him to join a Saturday game at the Marsh Lane pitch. Kofi says yes before he has time to think of an excuse, and he regrets it a little.
On Friday night, Kofi packs his football bag and leaves it by the door. When Saturday comes, the decision has already been made, and there is nothing left to argue about.
After the game, Kofi sits on the wet grass, muddy and out of breath. He has scored one goal by accident, and he is happier than he has been all week.
A small promise to another person can carry you when your own wish is weak. You may not get up for yourself, but you will often get up for somebody else.
Make your promises specific, with a time, a place and a name. “Let's meet sometime” rarely happens, but “See you at the park gate at ten” almost always does.
When you do not feel like going out, remember that it is usually easier than it seemed from the sofa. Most people feel better afterwards, even if they felt worse beforehand.

Mae at the library has heard Grace read a few lines out loud, and she asks whether Grace would read to the children on Thursdays. Grace says that she will think about it, and she says yes the same afternoon.
At home, Grace practises the story, with a deep voice for the bear and a squeaky one for the mouse. She feels silly at first, and then she realises that she is enjoying herself.
On Thursday, a dozen small children sit in a circle on the library carpet and gaze up at Grace. When she finishes the story, one boy asks whether the bear is her friend, and she laughs out loud.
Grace walks home through the park with her back straight and her head up. She feels taller than she did that morning, because somebody wanted her to be there.
Being needed and being loved are both good reasons to get up, and you can have both at once. When her grandson Theo visits, Grace gets both before nine o'clock.
Theo draws a picture of Grace as a stick figure holding an enormous book. She pins it to her fridge, where she can see it each morning and remember who she is.
Dev asks Grace to hold the ladder while he cuts a high branch in his garden. It is only a ten-minute job, but she feels useful, and he gives her three tomatoes as thanks.
A small act of kindness, such as taking soup to a sick neighbour, makes their day brighter and yours too. Grace discovers that giving can be as energising as receiving.
There is a limit, because being needed must not turn into being used up. A good reason gives you energy as well as taking it, so it is fine to say no sometimes.
On his day off, Kofi helps Abena carry a heavy sofa up three flights of stairs. His arms ache, and she laughs and pays him in pizza, but he feels useful for the first time in months.
Put one thing in your week that you really look forward to, such as a swim, a call with a friend or a class. It acts like a post in the ground that the rest of the week is tied to.
A week with no landmarks can feel like a long, flat road across an empty plain. There is nothing to walk towards, so every day looks exactly like the one before it.
Grace draws her week on a sheet of paper and sees that it now has three landmarks. There is the Tuesday walk, the Thursday story and the Sunday call from Ruth.
Kofi draws his own week, and he sees two landmarks, football on Saturday and cooking on Sunday. In between there are long, empty gaps, and he knows exactly where his phone fills them.
Look at the longest empty gap in your week and put one small thing into it. It could be a phone call, a swim or a class, and it should be something that you want to do.
On a quiet Wednesday, Grace finds that she is not lonely. She is looking forward to Thursday, and the anticipation makes today feel lighter too.

A regular class, such as a swim, a choir or a language lesson, gives you a place to go and people who recognise you. After a few weeks, the other members will begin to ask where you were if you miss a session.
Grace and Ruth agree on a regular time for their Sunday call, and now Theo joins in with his drawing of the week. The call has become the happy end of Grace's week.
Do not try to fill every day, because too many plans can feel like a to-do list. Two or three landmarks in a week are usually enough, and the space between them is useful too.
Try to keep one day each week with no plans at all. It stops your landmarks from becoming a list of jobs, and it leaves room for whatever you feel like doing.
Choose goals that are so small that you cannot fail. When a goal is easy, you will do it, and then you can let it grow.
Goals that you can finish in a single day give you a feeling of achievement every evening. A goal that takes a year gives you that feeling only once, and rather late.
Each morning Grace writes three tiny jobs: water the plants, read ten pages and walk to the postbox. By lunchtime she has usually finished them, and she feels ridiculously pleased.
Kofi's first tiny goal is to wash his dishes before he leaves for work. It takes five minutes, and coming home to a clean kitchen makes the whole flat feel calmer.
When you do not feel like starting, begin with the smallest possible part. If you want to go for a walk, put on your shoes, and nothing else is required yet.
Try the five-minute rule, which means telling yourself that you can stop after five minutes. Starting is the hard part, and once you have begun, you often want to carry on.
A big job can feel impossible, like a mountain of laundry. Fold one shirt first, and the mountain becomes a little smaller and a little more friendly.
Gentle goals grow by inches, and not by miles. When this week's goal feels easy, add a very small piece next week, and keep adding slowly.
If you miss a day, that is not a failure, because the chain of ticks can start again tomorrow. What matters is not a perfect record, but how quickly you come back.
In the evening, Grace and Kofi each look at their lists with a few ticks on them. Neither day was exciting, but each of them feels that the day was well spent.
Being bored and having no purpose are different things. Boredom says, “I want something to do,” and noticing which feeling you have is a helpful first step.
Boredom is uncomfortable, but it can be a door. Every parent has seen a bored child suddenly invent a brilliant game, because the mind needs a little empty space before it creates.
Boredom is a hungry feeling, and it wants something to do. A flat feeling that nothing matters is different, and if it lasts for weeks, it deserves more careful attention.
Sometimes you are not short of reasons but simply short of sleep. If you have been working hard or sleeping badly, rest first, and then ask yourself again whether you have a reason.
After a hard week of night shifts, Kofi sleeps for ten hours on Sunday. When he wakes, the world looks lighter, and he realises how much of his gloom was tiredness.
Slowing down to enjoy a small pleasure, such as a cup of tea, gives the day its taste. Most of us drink the tea without noticing, and then wonder where the day went.
Doing nothing on purpose, without guilt, is very different from scrolling without noticing. Sit by the window and watch the rain, and let your mind wander wherever it wants.
One morning, Grace eats a ripe pear very slowly, noticing the smell, the sweetness and the juice. She realises that she had been eating without tasting for years.
Kofi decides that Sunday afternoon, after the cooking, is for resting. He lies in the park with his eyes closed, and he stops feeling guilty about doing nothing.
Rest charges the battery that every reason runs on. Taking enough of it is not a break from your plan, because it is a part of the plan.
Adults often forget how to play, because everything we do seems to need a purpose. Doing something purely for fun, such as blowing bubbles, can give your energy back.
Games with other people, such as board games, cards or a silly quiz, are a cheerful reason to meet. Nobody minds who wins, and the laughing is the real prize.
In the shop on the high street, Grace buys a cheap box of watercolour paints. She cannot draw, but she wants to paint the birds from her window, and she is going to try.
Grace paints a robin, and it looks rather like a tomato with legs. She laughs, pins it up anyway and enjoys it more than she expected.
Being a beginner is perfectly fine, because everyone starts without skill. It may feel uncomfortable, but it is where every skilled person once stood.
Grace joins a Wednesday class for beginners at the community centre. She sits among strangers with her smudged paper, and she remembers what it feels like to be the pupil.
Kofi borrows Yaw's old guitar and learns his first chord from a chart. It sounds terrible, and his fingers hurt, but he feels like a child with a new toy.
Wobbly pots and wrong chords are evidence that you tried, and trying is the point. A shelf of imperfect things is better than an empty shelf.
Children do not mind being bad at things, because they are too busy enjoying them. We can borrow that attitude, and we may find it fits us better than we expected.
After three weeks, Kofi can play three chords, and he can even manage a tune that he recognises. It is not beautiful, but it is his, and he plays it twice just to hear it.
Dev, Grace's neighbour, grows tomatoes in large pots, and he checks them every morning. A living thing that needs you gives the day a very gentle kind of structure.
Dev gives Grace a small pot, a bag of soil and a few tomato seeds. He shows her how deep to push them, and she carries the pot home like a baby.
On the sixth morning a tiny green seedling pushes through the soil, and Grace gasps out loud. Each day she checks to see whether it has grown, and each day she is delighted.
Grace now waters her seedling every morning, and she finds herself getting up a little earlier to do it. Her mornings finally have a job that needs her.
Herbs such as basil, mint and parsley grow well on a window sill, even in a very small flat. They are easy to look after, and you can taste the reward on the same day.
An animal that depends on you can give you a reason to get up, because it needs feeding and walking every day. However, a pet is not right for everyone, and that is perfectly all right.
Dev's sister has a small dog called Biscuit who needs a walk on Mondays, when she is at work. Grace offers to take him, and soon Biscuit is waiting for her at the gate, wagging his tail.
A pet is a big promise that can last for many years, so think about it carefully. There are other ways to enjoy animals, such as walking a neighbour's dog or helping at a shelter.
Kofi brings home a spider plant, which Yaw promises is almost impossible to kill. He waters it every Sunday, and he is secretly proud when it grows a new baby plant.
In late summer, Grace's tomato plant produces its first red fruit. She and Dev share it, sliced, with a little salt, and neither of them says anything for a moment.
One night Kofi asks his manager, Ms Okoro, whether he could learn how the stock system works. He expects her to say no, but she smiles and says that she has been waiting for someone to ask.
Ms Okoro agrees to teach Kofi the system on quiet nights, for one hour at a time. The screens are confusing at first, but she is patient, and he starts to see how the whole warehouse fits together.
While counting boxes, Kofi finds that a whole shelf has the wrong label. He fixes the record, and the small win makes the rest of the night feel better.
Learning a skill at work gives you a path to follow. Kofi starts to see where his job could lead, and he wears a new badge for the stock team.
You may not be able to change your job, but you can often change how you look at it. Search for something to learn, a person to help or a small thing to improve.
Money is a real worry for many people, and nobody should pretend that it is not. If you are struggling to pay your bills, a hobby is not the answer, and it is sensible to seek practical help.
Many good reasons cost nothing at all, and some of them are the best that life has to give. A sunset from a hill, a walk along a river and a talk with a friend are all free.
Your local library will lend you books, music and often films without charging anything. It is also warm and quiet, and it often has events that anyone can join.
Make a list in your notebook of the free pleasures near your home. You might include a park, a market, a museum with free entry and a bench with a good view.
One afternoon, Grace and Kofi both stop at the noticeboard near the bakery, and they begin to read the free events together. It is the first time that they have talked for longer than a minute.
Choose one thing to look forward to for each month of the year. They do not have to be big, but together they turn a blank year into a path with landmarks.
Grace puts a star on a Saturday in June, and she writes the word “sea” beside it. She has not been to the seaside in six years, and she is already thinking about the sound of the waves.
Kofi circles the date of Abena's birthday dinner in August. He decides to cook her gran's stew for the whole family, and he starts to practise a little each Sunday.
A wish is much more likely to happen when it has a date next to it. Ring the day on the calendar, tell a friend about it, and you will feel the pull of it growing as it approaches.
Each evening, write down three good things from the day, however small they may be. It trains your eyes to notice what went well, and over time the list becomes a treasure.
Some people keep their good things in a jar, one note for each day. On a heavy morning, you can pull out a few notes and remember that good days really do happen.
One evening, Grace's list says that Dev gave her a tomato, that Theo drew her a rabbit and that the sun came out. She realises how many small kindnesses she used to miss.

It is never too late to begin something new, whatever your age. Many people have started a course, a language or an instrument in their seventies, and they usually say that they wish they had started sooner.
Kofi asks Grace whether she would look at a letter that he has written for a stock-control course. She takes out her old red pen with a smile, and he realises that she is still very much a teacher.
Kofi walks to the postbox and drops in his letter before he can change his mind. Whether he is accepted or not, he is proud of himself for having tried.
Some days you will fail to get up, however good your plans are. That is not the end of the story, because you can begin again tomorrow.
After a week of rain and a heavy cold, Grace stays in bed for three mornings in a row. The old heaviness is back, and she feels as though all her progress has vanished.
Grace imagines that a friend has told her the same story, and she asks what she would say. She would say that it is all right to rest, so she says it to herself.
After a difficult shift, Kofi slides back into scrolling and loses a whole weekend to it. The old habit is strong, and he feels angry with himself on Monday.
When you have slipped, take the smallest step you can think of. Open the curtain, drink a glass of water or put on your shoes, and let the next step follow when it is ready.

If you feel that nothing interests you for many weeks, or if your sleep and appetite have changed a lot, please talk to a doctor. Low mood is common and often treatable, and this book is not a replacement for medical advice.

If you ever feel that life is not worth living, or that you might hurt yourself, please tell someone straight away. Contact your local emergency service or a helpline, because trained people are ready to listen.
On a Saturday morning, Grace and Kofi sit on a bench with warm rolls from the bakery. After a while, Kofi admits that he finds the mornings hard, and the words come out more easily than he expected.
Grace tells Kofi that she finds mornings hard as well, and that she has done so for months. He is relieved to learn that he is not strange, and she is relieved to have said it.
Grace and Kofi decide to take a walk together every Saturday morning, ending at the bakery. Each of them now has a reason that depends on the other, and neither wants to let the other down.
A reason that works in spring may fade by autumn, and that is normal. Look at your list every few months, drop what has lost its pull and add something new.
Mae invites Grace to give a short talk about garden birds at the library. People ask her good questions, and she realises that she is still a teacher, only now she teaches because she wants to.
When winter comes, the outdoor reasons are harder to enjoy, so look for warm ones indoors. A pot of soup, a good book and a lamp can be as good as a summer walk.
An email comes, and Kofi gets a place on the stock-control course. Ms Okoro changes his shifts so that he can go on Thursday evenings, and he is nervous and proud at the same time.
Let us gather the main ideas before we say goodbye. Look for small reasons, share your days with other people, and stay curious about the world.
Remember also to set goals that are small and gentle, to rest when you are tired, and to play now and then. When you slip, begin again, because starting again is a skill that everybody needs.
Your list will not look like Grace's, or like Kofi's, and it should not. A reason is a personal thing, and the best one is the one that makes you want to put your feet on the floor.
A year on, Grace still drinks her tea on the doorstep at dawn, and Kofi still walks past on his way home. He stops, hands her a warm roll and sits down for a moment.
Tonight, before you go to bed, open your notebook and write down one small reason to get up tomorrow. It might be a cup of tea, a message to a friend or a walk to the corner.
Tomorrow morning, in two houses on Alder Road, two curtains will open at sunrise. Your alarm will ring as usual, but this time you will have something waiting for you on the other side of it.
C1C2: An alarm clock is very good at waking you, yet it has never persuaded anyone that the day ahead is worth entering. That quiet wish to get up comes only from having a reason, something waiting on the other side of the morning that you would honestly like to meet. This book is about finding yours, and about learning to recognise it when it quietly arrives on an ordinary day.

Most of us have pressed the snooze button at least once, trusting that ten more minutes under the blanket will somehow repair the morning. It rarely does, because the problem was never a shortage of minutes but a shortage of anything pulling us out of the warmth. The bed is comfortable, the day is vague, and the sensible animal inside us chooses comfort.

Some mornings feel as heavy as wet sand, and the simple act of swinging your legs out of bed seems to require a decision of enormous weight. This happens to nearly everyone at some time, and it says far less about your character than you might fear. A heavy morning is a piece of weather rather than a verdict, and weather, as everyone knows, changes.

Look around any bus stop at seven o'clock on a dark winter morning and you will see a collection of tired faces, each person privately wondering why they are there. Almost everybody has felt the heaviness that you sometimes feel, even those who look cheerful and sound brisk. Knowing that you are in good company will not solve the problem, but it removes the shame, and shame is a heavy load of its own.

An alarm pushes you out of bed from behind, like a hand in the small of your back, whereas a reason pulls you forward like a rope tied to the bow of a boat. Both can move you across the water, but only the second makes you want to be moved. A good deal of this book is about finding the rope and learning how to tie it to something worth reaching.

When you were small, you probably leapt out of bed on birthdays and on the first morning of a holiday, without any alarm at all. Nobody had to push you, because something delightful was waiting on the far side of the bedroom door and you could hardly bear to be late. That feeling has not vanished with age; it has only become quieter, and a little harder to hear.

A duty is something you carry on your back, and it grows heavier the longer you carry it without knowing why. A reason is more like a kite, which rises on the wind and asks nothing of you except that you hold the string. Plenty of good lives contain both, but on a difficult morning it is the kite that will lift you.

This book will invite you to try a number of small experiments, and you will need somewhere to record what happens. A cheap notebook and a pen are all the equipment required, and the best place to keep them is beside your bed, where they cannot be forgotten. Nothing you write needs to be neat, clever or even complete, because the notebook is only for you.

Many people believe that a reason to get up must be a grand purpose, something worthy of a speech or a biography. It need not be anything of the kind, since a reason has only to be sturdy enough to carry you through today. Tomorrow you can find another one, and the next day another, and the path will gradually form behind you as you walk.

Your first task is a very small one, and you can complete it without leaving the bed: tomorrow morning, before you move, simply notice how you feel. There is no need to judge the feeling, argue with it or fix it, because noticing is how any honest journey begins. Write down a few words in your notebook afterwards, and then turn the page to meet Grace, who has been noticing the same thing for months.

Grace is sixty-eight, and last spring she retired from a school where she had taught for forty years. At nine o'clock on a Monday morning she stands in her silent kitchen on Alder Road, holding an empty mug and wondering what, exactly, the rest of the day is for. For four decades the question had always answered itself, and now it simply hangs in the air like steam.

At nine o'clock exactly, Grace still hears the school bell ringing somewhere in her head, although it has not rung for her in months. Her body remembers a rhythm of lessons, corridors and thirty upturned faces that her life no longer contains. It is a strange and rather touching thing to remain loyal to a timetable that has quietly stopped existing without telling anyone.

For the first time in decades, the calendar on Grace's kitchen wall has nothing written on it at all. She had dreamed of this freedom for years, picturing long afternoons and unhurried breakfasts, but now the white squares look less like a gift than a question nobody has asked her to answer. Freedom, she is discovering, is a great deal easier to imagine in advance than to fill when it finally arrives.

The mornings have grown so long that Grace has begun to watch the clock, as she once watched a restless class on the last afternoon of term. She tells herself that she is resting, but a quiet and honest voice reminds her that she is mostly waiting, although she could not say for what. The minutes crawl past one by one, and none of them seems to belong to her in any way that matters.

Grace's daughter Ruth lives in a city four hours away by train, and she telephones faithfully every Sunday evening. For the other six days of the week the telephone sits silent beside the photograph of Ruth and her small son Theo, and Grace has begun to notice the silence the way one notices a clock that has stopped. She never complains, since Ruth is busy and loving, but the quiet is real all the same.

Grace finds an old red marking pen at the back of a drawer and holds it for a while, as one might hold a medal. It is not the marking that she misses so much as the feeling of being useful, of being the person to whom a puzzled child turned and said, “Please, can you help?” Nobody asks her anything now, and she did not realise how much she had liked it.

Grace has started to stretch her errands, walking slowly to the shops and back and buying one small item at a time so that the trips will last longer. A single loaf of bread can now fill most of a morning, which she finds faintly comic and faintly sad. She does not feel that the time is well spent, only that it is spent.

One morning, while washing a cup, Grace realises that she has been answering the radio presenter out loud, and with some energy. She laughs at herself, because it really is rather funny, but a quieter part of her understands what the habit means. A person who answers a radio, she thinks, is usually a person who has too few ordinary conversations in the course of a week.

Late one night, sitting on the edge of her bed with the lamp switched off, Grace allows herself to ask a question she has been avoiding for months. She does not ask what she ought to do with her retirement, which would have an easy and dutiful answer, but what she actually has to get up for. The silence that follows is not frightening, as she had feared it might be, but only very quiet and very honest.

The very next day Grace buys a plain blue notebook at the stationer's and writes her question across the top of the first page in her careful teacher's handwriting. It is the first thing she has planned in months, and she is surprised to find that she is rather proud of it. Somewhere between the shop and the kitchen table, the morning has started to feel as though it belongs to someone.

Kofi is twenty-four, and he works the night shift at the Eastgate warehouse on the edge of town. While the rest of the city sleeps, he pushes trolleys of boxes from one end of an enormous building to the other, under lights that never dim. It is steady work and he does it well, but it has turned his days upside down.

Kofi rides the bus home at dawn, his forehead against the cool window, passing crowds of people on their way to work. They are starting their day while he is finishing his, and he feels a full step out of time with the world, like a guest who has arrived at the wrong party. The feeling is not unpleasant, exactly, but it is lonely, and it makes the ride seem longer than it is.

Kofi eats his breakfast at seven in the morning, just as the sunlight spreads across his small kitchen table. For him this is the quiet end of a long day, and for nearly everyone else on his street it is the energetic beginning of one. He eats slowly, listening to neighbours' doors close and engines start, and he feels like an observer rather than a participant.

After a few hours of broken sleep, Kofi wakes and reaches straight for his phone, as automatically as a person reaches for a glass of water. He promises himself that he will look for five minutes, and then the afternoon quietly dissolves around him while his thumb keeps moving. When he finally puts the phone down, he cannot remember a single thing that he has seen.

Kofi watches video after video, though if he were honest he would admit that he enjoys hardly any of them. It is simply easier to let the screen decide what comes next than to face the open question of what he actually wants to do with his free hours. The phone offers him constant company without any real companionship, like a crowd of strangers who never ask his name.

By five o'clock in the afternoon the daylight is already fading, and Kofi has accomplished nothing except the washing of one mug. He feels heavy, restless and faintly ashamed, though he could not easily explain what he has done wrong. The wasted hours sit in his chest like a stone, and they make the evening shift ahead look even longer.

Most of Kofi's friends work during the day, so their replies to his messages arrive hours late, if they arrive at all. By the time they are free and in the mood to talk, he is already on a bus heading back to the warehouse, and the conversation dies before it begins. None of this is anybody's fault, yet the gaps between messages feel wider each week.

Kofi's sister Abena calls him on video one afternoon and asks, in her usual cheerful way, what he has done with his day. He opens his mouth to answer and realises, to his own surprise, that there is nothing to report apart from sleeping, scrolling and eating. Abena does not judge him, but her gentle silence is louder than any lecture could have been.

Kofi does not hate his job, and his colleagues at Eastgate are decent, hard-working people who share their biscuits and their jokes. The trouble is that when he searches his mind for something to anticipate, he finds only two items, payday and sleep. Neither of them, he suspects, is the sort of thing that a person is supposed to live for.

After Abena's call, Kofi finds a yellow sticky note and writes a single question on it, which he presses firmly to the door of his fridge: what am I looking forward to? He has no answer yet, and the note looks a little silly in his untidy kitchen, but the question is at last out of his head and in front of his eyes. Every time he reaches for the milk, it will be there to greet him.

People often imagine that a reason to get up must be something large and important, like a career or a mission. In fact it can be a cup of excellent coffee, a plant that needs watering or a friend who will be waiting at the corner café. Small reasons are not second-rate, because a day is made almost entirely of small moments, and these are the ones we actually live in.

A single brick is not much to look at, and no one has ever been impressed by one, yet a handsome wall is made of nothing else. In the same way, a handful of modest reasons can add up to a day well worth starting, even if no individual reason would persuade you alone. The trick is to stop waiting for one enormous stone and to begin collecting bricks.

Try to gather about three small reasons for each day, so that no single one has to bear the entire weight of your morning. If one of them falls through, as even the best-laid plans sometimes do, the other two will still be standing to hold you up. A table with three legs does not collapse the moment one of them wobbles.

A grand purpose can feel as remote as the summit of a mountain, and about as helpful on a cold morning when you are still in your pyjamas. A small reason, by contrast, is a handhold within easy reach, something you can grasp before breakfast and use to pull yourself up the next step. Climbers rarely think about the top; they think about where their hands go next.

Someone who is waiting for you is already a perfectly good reason to get up, and it hardly matters that the occasion is only a chat over a cup of tea. Human beings are built to respond to one another, and the thought of a friendly face on the other side of a table can pull us through a door that nothing else would open. Seen in that light, a promise to meet a friend is a small act of self-care.

Looking forward to a really good breakfast is a thoroughly respectable reason to get out of bed, and no one is obliged to be impressed by it. The only test of a reason is whether it works, and the smell of toast has been moving people across cold bedroom floors for centuries. There is no hierarchy of reasons, and nobody will give you extra marks for choosing something solemn.

A story that you are halfway through is a wonderful reason to wake up, or at least a reason to get comfortably settled with a cup of tea. You want to know what happens next, and that simple wanting is the beginning of energy, the spark that turns a flat hour into a lively one. Many readers have been pulled out of a heavy mood by nothing more than the last chapter of a novel.

Small pleasures do not have to be productive, educational or impressive in any way, and it is a mistake to demand that they should be. They only have to be yours, and they only have to make the day feel a little more worth entering than it did when you opened your eyes. A pile of pebbles on a beach is useless, and nobody who has built one has ever regretted it.

Under her question, Grace slowly writes her first honest answer: the library on Hill Road opens at ten, and she has always loved the smell of its shelves. It is not a profound discovery, and she feels slightly shy writing it down, but the thought of walking through those doors makes her stand a little straighter. She underlines it twice, as she used to underline the best sentences in her pupils' essays.

Kofi's first answer, scribbled beneath the question on his yellow note, is the little bakery on the corner of his street. When he walks past in the late afternoon, the first hot loaves are just coming out of the oven, and the warm smell follows him for half a block. It is only bread, but it is the first thing in weeks that has made him walk faster instead of slower.

Look back over the past twelve months and write down five things that you genuinely looked forward to while they were still in the future. They can be tiny, and they do not need to sound impressive, because the aim is simply to collect evidence about what has pulled you forward before. Your own history is the best place to start, since it is the one source of information that nobody can argue with.

Old photographs, saved messages and even receipts can remind you of days that you enjoyed far more than you recall. Look through them slowly, and notice not the places where you posed but the moments where you forgot the camera was there and smiled without effort. Memory tends to flatten the past into a grey blur, while a single snapshot can make the colours return.
