Think back to what you loved when you were about ten years old, before anyone had told you what a sensible person should enjoy. Some of those early passions have never really gone away, and they sit quietly in the back of your mind, patiently waiting for an invitation. A child who drew maps or built dens or collected shells is often still inside the adult, politely tapping on the glass.

Think about the times when an hour slipped by without your noticing, because you were so thoroughly absorbed in what you were doing that you forgot to be hungry. Psychologists sometimes call this state flow, but you do not need a technical word to recognise the feeling of the world narrowing to a single pleasant task. Such moments are valuable clues, because they show you where your attention goes when it is free to choose.

When Grace makes her list, she is struck by how many lines turn out to be about teaching, and about one particular moment above all the others. She remembers a shy boy who finally understood fractions after weeks of frowning, and the astonished delight on his face still makes her smile at the kitchen table. It was never the lessons themselves that she loved so much as the instant when a puzzled mind came suddenly alight.

Kofi's list is much shorter than Grace's, and he writes it on the back of an old envelope, a little embarrassed by its brevity. Even so, every line on it is real: football on a muddy pitch, his gran's cooking on Sunday afternoons, and the shiver of hearing a really good song for the first time. He looks at the envelope and realises that he used to have a much fuller life than he thought.

Look at your list carefully and ask what the items have in common, treating yourself as a detective with a promising pile of clues. You may find a pattern, such as being with people, making things with your hands, moving your body or learning something new, and that pattern is a compass that points towards your own kind of reason. Two people can write completely different lists and still discover the same word circled twice.

Some of the things on your list may be gone for good, perhaps because a job has ended, a friend has moved away or a body no longer does what it used to do. It is perfectly natural to grieve for them a little before you go looking for replacements, and there is no need to hurry through the sadness in order to appear positive. Honest sorrow clears the ground, whereas pretending to feel nothing only leaves the weeds.

Pick the one item on your list that still feels warm when you think about it, even if only faintly, like a coal that has not quite gone out. Then ask how a very small piece of it, perhaps ten minutes or a single phone call, could fit into the coming week. Nobody needs to rebuild a whole life at once, since a single spark is enough to begin with.

In two different kitchens, only a few streets apart, Grace circles the words “finding things out” while Kofi circles the single word “cooking”. Neither of them has the faintest idea that the other exists, and neither expects much from the experiment, but each of them plans one small first step for the following day. It is not much of a plan, yet it is more of a plan than either has had for months.

Curiosity is a kind of fuel, because a good question gives the mind somewhere to go and a reason to arrive there. You do not need a library of enquiries or a university degree, since a single fresh one each day is enough to keep the engine turning over. Children run on this fuel all day long, which is why they seem so much less weary of the world than we sometimes are.

Write each question that crosses your mind on a small slip of paper, and drop it into a jar that lives on the kitchen shelf. Whenever you have a spare quarter of an hour, pull one out at random and go looking for the answer, whether in a book, on a walk or from a knowledgeable friend. The jar becomes a little treasury of future mornings, each slip a tiny promise that tomorrow will have something in it.

One morning a small brown bird lands on Grace's garden fence and begins to sing, and she realises with some embarrassment that she has no idea what it is. It is a curious sensation for a woman who spent forty years being the person in the room who knew the answers. Instead of feeling foolish, however, she finds herself leaning forward, and her heart gives a small, unfamiliar skip of interest.

At the Hill Road library, a young assistant named Mae finds Grace a thick guide to garden birds and asks, with real interest, what she has seen. Grace is surprised by how glad she is to be on the receiving end of help for once, after a lifetime of being the one who gave it. Being a learner again feels like putting on an old coat and discovering that it still fits.

Learning something new is rewarding in a way that very little else is, because you can actually feel yourself improving from one day to the next. Each morning Grace recognises a little more of what she sees at the window, and she marks each newly identified bird in her guide with a small and satisfying tick. Progress that you can see is a wonderful engine, and it runs even on very cold mornings.

After a week of patient watching, Grace finally finds her mystery visitor on a page of the guide, and she says its name aloud to the empty kitchen. It is a dunnock, a modest brown bird that prefers hedges and low bushes, and it turns out to be far more interesting than it looks at first glance. She feels the quiet triumph of a detective who has solved a small and charming case.

Kofi finally asks the baker the question that has been in his head for weeks, which is why the bread on the corner tastes so much better than any other. The baker laughs and explains that the secret is mostly time, because the dough is left to rise slowly for many hours before it ever goes near the oven. Kofi walks home thinking that good things, like good bread, seem to need a little patience.

Following one question wherever it happens to lead, with no deadline and no examination at the end, is a form of play for the mind. You may start with a small brown bird and finish an hour later reading about the migration of birds across a different continent, quite unable to remember how you got there. That wandering is not a waste of time but the very purpose of curiosity.

Do not be afraid to put your questions to other people, for most of us are delighted to be asked about the things we know and love. A neighbour who has grown roses for thirty years, a retired engineer on the bus, or a shopkeeper with a special interest can open a door in a single sentence that would take you hours to open alone. A good question is also a small compliment, a way of telling the other person that their knowledge is worth having.

Every answer you find has a way of bringing a fresh question trailing behind it, like a kite tail that grows longer the more you pull. That chain of questions is a rope tied to tomorrow, and each link makes it a little easier to believe that the next day will contain something worth discovering. Grace looks at her notebook, sees four crossed-out questions and one new one, and is delighted to find that she cannot wait for the morning.

Kofi makes a simple resolution: he will cook one new dish every week, and he will do it on Sunday, his one properly free afternoon. Before long he finds himself looking forward to Sundays, which is something he cannot remember saying about any day of the week in years. A plan does not have to be ambitious in order to alter the shape of an entire life.

At the bottom of a kitchen drawer, Kofi finds a stained recipe card in his gran's looping handwriting, giving the method for her famous groundnut stew. He decides to cook it first, even though he has never made it himself, and he reads her instructions as though she were standing beside him. Some recipes carry far more than ingredients, and this one carries the sound of her laugh.

Chopping, stirring and tasting are simple, repetitive steps, and each one anchors Kofi's mind firmly in the room. For the first time in weeks his thoughts are not leaping from one glowing screen to the next, because the onion demands his attention and the pot will not forgive neglect. It is an odd and rather lovely kind of relief to be needed, for a while, by nothing grander than a bubbling stew.

Kofi holds up the finished bowl to the camera on a video call, and Abena shrieks that it looks exactly like Gran's. He feels a warm flush of pride that he has not felt in a long time, and when she begs him to send her the recipe, he realises that he has something to give. Sharing what you have made turns a private pleasure into a bridge between two people.

Using your hands, whether to cook, to garden or to mend something broken, brings a calm and particular kind of satisfaction. The mind rests while the fingers work, and at the end of it there is something real that you can look at, smell or sit upon. Our ancestors spent most of their waking hours making things, and some quiet part of us still seems to expect to.

Grace discovers a torn cushion cover in the back of a cupboard and mends it with a needle and thread, using stitches that she has not made since her own daughter was small. It takes a single hour, and when she has finished she realises that it is the first thing she has fully completed in weeks. She places the cushion on her armchair and looks at it far longer than a cushion deserves.

A finished object is a satisfying thing, because you can point at it and say, “I did that,” which is quite unlike the endless chores that are never really complete. Dishes return, emails multiply and floors get dirty again, but a loaf of bread or a mended chair stays mended. There is a quiet dignity in leaving a visible mark on the world, however small it may be.

Grace's neighbour Dev, a cheerful man who grows tomatoes in the garden next door, hands her an old wooden stool and a sheet of sandpaper over the fence. He shows her how to sand along the grain rather than against it, and then he wisely leaves her to it. By lunchtime she has rubbed the wood so smooth that she cannot stop stroking it.

Busy hands can quieten a busy mind, which is why so many people find repetitive crafts such as knitting, sanding or kneading soothing. You do not have to be talented, because the rhythm does most of the work, carrying your thoughts gently away from whatever was worrying them. Afterwards, you may find that the worry has shrunk a little, as though it had been left out in the rain.

At the end of the week, make a note in your notebook of one thing that your hands have made, mended or tended. It might be a meal, a mended shirt, a bunch of flowers in a jam jar or a shelf that is finally straight. Reading the list on a heavy morning will remind you that you are a person who makes things, and such people usually have something to get up for.

Before you go to bed, set out a small treat for the morning, such as a favourite biscuit on a plate beside the kettle. When you wake, something kind is already waiting for you, placed there by an earlier and wiser version of yourself. It is a tiny gift from last night to tomorrow, and it costs almost nothing.

Setting out your cup, spoon and tea bag the night before removes a whole row of small decisions from a tired morning. A sleepy mind finds even tiny choices surprisingly hard, so it is kind to make the first steps of the day as easy as possible. When the path is already laid, your feet are more likely to follow it.

Make the first half hour of your day as agreeable as you possibly can. Play music that you love, sit in your favourite chair and drink something warm, and the rest of the morning will feel noticeably lighter than it would have done if you had rushed straight into it. A good beginning does not guarantee a good day, of course, but it certainly helps and it is entirely within your power.

Give the first ten minutes of your day to something slow, quiet and pleasant, without any hurry at all. Nobody is chasing you, and nothing of importance will collapse if you simply sit with a warm cup and look out of the window at the weather. Those ten unhurried minutes set the tone, the way the first few notes of a song tell you what sort of music you are about to hear.

Grace drapes a soft blanket over her armchair, props her bird book on the window sill and puts the binoculars within easy reach. The next morning, for the first time in months, she finds herself hurrying to the kitchen to make her tea, impatient to take up her place. A small corner of a room, arranged with love, can turn the hardest part of the day into the best.

Kofi's morning begins in the early afternoon, after he has slept through the best of the daylight, and it would be easy to say that none of this advice applies to him. In fact the idea works at any hour of the clock, since a pleasant beginning matters whenever your own day happens to start. The sun is not the point; the point is the first ten minutes after you wake.

Kofi begins to buy a small loaf from the corner bakery on his way to work, and he saves a thick slice with butter for the moment he wakes. It is a tiny and uncomplicated pleasure, but it gets him out of bed faster than any alarm has ever managed. Anticipation, he is discovering, is a good deal more persuasive than discipline, and a great deal more pleasant.

Each evening, name one thing that you are looking forward to tomorrow and write it in your notebook, however plain it may seem. It does not have to be exciting; a bowl of good soup, a phone call or a favourite programme will do very nicely. Going to sleep with something to wake up for is a kind of gift that you can give yourself every single night.

A calm routine is not the same thing as a strict one, and anyone who tries to turn the morning into a military drill will probably give up by Thursday. It is simply a collection of small habits that you actually enjoy, arranged in an order that feels natural. The test is whether it feels more like a comfortable path or a rulebook, and only the path will last.

Rules that are too rigid will eventually snap, whereas a good routine is flexible and bends in the wind like a young tree. It should be gentle enough to forgive a bad day, so that a single missed morning does not bring the entire plan crashing down. You are not a machine, and your routine should not pretend that you are.

Open the curtains the moment you get up, and if you can, step outside for a minute or two. Daylight tells your body that the day has begun, and for most people it is one of the gentlest and most effective ways of waking up properly. It is free, it is always available, even on a grey morning, and it asks nothing of you but a little courage at the door.

Grace begins to drink her morning tea on the front step in her dressing gown, with the door open behind her and the day laid out in front. The street looks quite different at that early hour, and she is surprised by how much is going on, from the milk float's hum to the neighbours' cat on the wall. She had lived on Alder Road for thirty years without once seeing it wake up.

A little movement each day often lifts the mood and adds to your energy, and it does not have to look anything like sport. A brisk walk to the end of the road is enough to start, and many people find that their thoughts untangle themselves as their legs find a rhythm. This book cannot promise a cure, but it can say that bodies and moods are connected, and that movement is a friend.

Kofi decides to get off the bus one stop early and walk the last ten minutes of his journey home. At first it feels like a pointless effort after a long night of lifting, but by the end of the week he is looking forward to the cool air and the smell of the bakery as it opens. His tired body, which he assumed wanted only to lie down, turns out to want to move as well.

Each morning on his way home, Kofi walks past Grace sitting on her doorstep with her mug and her binoculars. At first they exchange only a nod, then a shy good morning, and before the month is out each of them is quietly looking out for the other as a pleasant fixed point of the day. Neither could have predicted that a few friendly syllables, repeated daily, would matter so much.

You do not need a gym membership, expensive shoes or a sporting past in order to begin. A walk to the end of your street and back is a perfectly respectable start, and you can add a lamp-post or two each week as your confidence grows. The goal is not to impress a doctor or a watch, but to teach your body that going outside is something it does.

Going to bed at roughly the same time each night makes mornings easier, because the body likes to know what to expect. Charge your phone on the far side of the room, where it cannot tempt you with one last glance in the dark or a sudden rush of news at midnight. Your sleep will not turn perfect overnight, but over a few weeks it should become noticeably kinder to you.

Try an unhurried hour of winding down before bed, with softer lights and nothing particularly exciting to read, watch or argue about. It sends a message to your body that the day's work is finished, that the world can manage without you for eight hours, and that it is safe to rest. The routine does not have to be elaborate, and a warm drink, a dim lamp and a few quiet minutes are quite enough.

Because Kofi sleeps during the day, he hangs thick curtains over his bedroom window and tapes a polite note to the door asking the postman not to knock. His room becomes dark and quiet, a small cave in the middle of a noisy afternoon, and he finds that his sleep grows deeper and more restful. Shift workers cannot always choose the hour of their sleep, but they can often choose its conditions.

Keep your bedside table beautifully simple, with a book, a glass of water and a notebook, but no glowing screen. It is much harder to scroll for an hour when there is nothing to scroll with, and a few pages of a story will usually send you off to sleep with a calmer mind. If you still lie awake some nights, do not be hard on yourself, because everyone does.

On the library noticeboard, between a lost cat and a piano for sale, Grace notices an advertisement for a Tuesday morning walking group that promises a warm welcome to all. She reads it three times and then walks away, because a nervous voice inside her suggests that she is too old, too shy and too late. For a whole week the little poster follows her around the house, quietly asking her what she is afraid of.

The following Tuesday, Grace puts on her sturdiest shoes and makes herself walk to the park gate, where a dozen people in coats are standing about in the cold. She feels more nervous than she did on her first day of teaching, and she says almost nothing, but she walks the entire route with the group. When she gets home she is astonished to find that she has survived it.

At the halfway bench, the leader of the group, a brisk and smiling woman named Ines, pours Grace a cup of tea from an enormous flask. She asks Grace her name and then actually uses it, which is a small kindness that Grace, as a former teacher, knows to be a rare and precious skill. By the time the cup is empty, she feels like a member of something rather than a visitor.

By the third week, Grace is five minutes late one rainy Tuesday, and when she arrives at the gate, out of breath, the others cry out that they were about to send a search party. She realises with a rush of warmth that she would have been missed, and that she is now a person whose absence is noticed. That is a far stronger reason to put on wet shoes than any amount of good advice.

Kofi's old friend Yaw asks him to join a casual Saturday game of football on the Marsh Lane pitch, and Kofi says yes before he has time to think up an excuse. By the evening he is already regretting it, because he is tired, out of practice and sure that he will be the slowest player on the field. A promise made quickly, however, is often the only kind that gets made at all.

On Friday night, before he leaves for his shift, Kofi packs his football bag and leaves it standing beside the front door like a patient dog. When Saturday morning comes and his tired brain begins to compose excuses, he finds that the decision was made hours ago by a more energetic version of himself. Preparing things the night before is a small trick, but it removes the argument before it has a chance to begin.

After the game, Kofi sits on the wet grass, muddy from head to foot and gasping for breath, while his friends tease him about the goal he scored by accident. He is exhausted and slightly bruised, yet he realises that he is happier than he has been at any point all week. The body, it seems, remembers how to enjoy itself even when the mind has forgotten.

A small promise to another person can carry you through the days when your own wish is weak. You may not be willing to get up for yourself on a drizzly morning, but you will very often get up because somebody is waiting at the gate. This is not a trick or a weakness; it is simply how human beings are wired, and there is no shame in using it.

Make your promises as specific as you can, with a time, a place and a name attached to each of them. “Let's meet sometime” is a warm sentiment that almost never happens, whereas “See you at the park gate at ten” is a plan that almost always does. Vagueness lets the days slide past, but a clear appointment gives the days a handle to grip.

When you do not feel at all like going out, remember that the journey is usually much easier than it seemed from the comfort of the sofa. Most people find that they feel better afterwards than they did before, even if the first ten minutes were an effort of will, and almost nobody regrets having turned up. The hardest part of any meeting is the doorway, so take a breath and walk through it.

Mae at the library has overheard Grace reading a few lines aloud to herself, and she asks whether Grace might like to read to the children on Thursday mornings. Grace says that she will think about it, which is what everyone says when they have already decided, and she telephones the library the same afternoon to accept. It is the first time in a year that anybody has asked her for something.

At home, Grace practises the story in her armchair, giving the bear a deep rumble and the mouse a squeak that makes her cough with laughter. She feels thoroughly silly at first, talking to the empty room, and then she realises that she has not enjoyed herself so much in a very long time. The teacher in her, which she had assumed was retired, has simply been waiting for the next performance.

On Thursday morning, a dozen small children settle in a circle on the library carpet and gaze up at Grace with round, serious eyes. When she finishes the story, a boy in a green jumper asks whether the bear is her friend, and she laughs so heartily that the whole circle starts laughing too. It is a long time since a room has been so warm, and she realises that she had missed the noise of children.

Grace walks home across the park with her back straight and her head held higher than it has been in months. She feels distinctly taller than she did that morning, and she cannot quite explain why, except that for an hour or two somebody wanted her to be exactly where she was. To be needed, even in a small way, appears to be a form of nourishment as real as bread.

Being needed and being loved are both excellent reasons to get up in the morning, and the happiest days contain a generous portion of each. When Grace's six-year-old grandson Theo comes to stay for a weekend, she receives both before nine o'clock, along with a great deal of jam on her sleeve. She realises that she has been missing not only the work of teaching but also the closeness of other people's lives.

Before he goes home, Theo draws a picture of his grandmother as a stick figure with a triumphant smile, holding an enormous book that is wider than she is. Grace pins it to her fridge door with a magnet shaped like a strawberry, where she will see it every morning while she waits for the kettle to boil. It is a small, wobbly reminder of who she is in the eyes of someone who loves her.

Dev leans over the fence one afternoon and asks whether Grace would be kind enough to hold his ladder while he cuts a high branch from his apple tree. It is only a ten-minute job, but she feels pleasantly useful, and he thanks her with three tomatoes that are still warm from the sun. Small favours between neighbours are like stitches in a piece of cloth, quietly holding the street together.

A small act of kindness, such as carrying a pot of soup to a neighbour who has been unwell, brightens their day and, quite unexpectedly, your own. Grace discovers on the doorstep that giving can be every bit as energising as receiving, and she walks home with a lightness she did not set out with. Kindness has this odd property of leaving more behind in the giver than it takes away.

There is, however, a limit, because being needed must never be allowed to curdle into being used up. A good reason gives you energy as well as taking it, and if a commitment leaves you exhausted and resentful week after week, it is not a reason but a burden in a pleasant costume. You are allowed to say no, and you are allowed to say it kindly.

On his day off, Kofi gives up his usual afternoon of scrolling to help Abena carry a monstrous sofa up three flights of stairs into her new flat. His arms ache and the sofa gets stuck at every corner, but she laughs and pays him in pizza, and he realises that he has not felt so useful in months. Being somebody's brother, he discovers, is also a perfectly good reason to get out of bed.

Put one thing in your week that you truly look forward to, such as a swim, a call with an old friend or an evening class. It acts like a post in the ground, giving the rest of the week something to be tied to, so that the days lean towards it instead of dissolving into each other. A week without a landmark can feel like a flat and featureless plain, across which it is hard to find any reason to walk.

A week with no landmarks can feel like a long, straight road across an empty plain, with no hill, no village and no signpost anywhere on the horizon. There is nothing to walk towards, so every day looks exactly like the one before it, and it becomes hard to say what has happened or when. A single tall signpost in the distance changes the whole journey, since it gives your feet a direction.

Grace draws her week on a large sheet of paper and sees, to her quiet delight, that it now has three firm landmarks. There is the Tuesday walk with Ines and the others, the Thursday story at the library, and the Sunday evening call from Ruth, each one marked in a different colour of pen. A month earlier the same page would have been blank, and she studies it as a gardener studies a bed that is finally beginning to fill.

Kofi draws his own week on the back of a bank letter and sees two clear landmarks, football on Saturday and the Sunday cooking afternoon. Between them stretch long, empty gaps of three or four days, and he knows with some embarrassment exactly which glowing rectangle usually fills them. Seeing the pattern on paper makes it easier to understand, and it is much harder to feel guilty about a gap that you can see how to fix.

Look carefully at the longest empty gap in your week and place one small, appealing event in the middle of it. It could be a phone call with a cousin, a swim at the local pool or a beginners' class, but it should be something that you actually want rather than something that you feel you ought to do. Even a modest landmark in the empty middle will reduce the length of the plain on either side.

On a quiet Wednesday afternoon, Grace notices with surprise that she is not lonely at all, even though she has spoken to nobody since the morning. She is looking forward to Thursday, and the anticipation seems to spread backwards through the week, making even this ordinary day feel lighter. Looking forward is a pleasure in itself, and it often lasts longer than the event.

A regular class, whether it is a swim, a choir or a language lesson, gives you both a place to be and a circle of people who recognise you. After a few weeks the other members begin to ask where you were when you miss a session, and that gentle expectation is worth more than any amount of willpower. Many people discover that the subject hardly matters, for it is the weekly company that really keeps them coming.

Grace and Ruth agree on a fixed time for their Sunday call, six o'clock sharp, and Theo now joins in each week with a drawing to hold up to the camera. What had been a pleasant duty on Ruth's part has become the bright end of Grace's week, something to prepare for and to talk about. A regular call is a little bridge that you rebuild every seven days, and each time it feels stronger.

Do not be tempted to fill every day of the week, because a diary crammed with appointments soon begins to feel like a list of chores. Two or three landmarks are usually enough, and the empty spaces between them are not failures but room to breathe, to rest and to be surprised. A landscape made entirely of mountains is exhausting, and nobody can live on the summit.

Try to keep one day of each week completely free of plans, and write the word “nothing” across it on the calendar with a flourish. It stops your landmarks from hardening into a list of obligations, and it leaves open a whole day in which you can follow whatever whim happens to arrive. Some of the best reasons turn up uninvited on days that were left empty on purpose.

Choose goals that are so small that you could hardly fail to reach them, such as reading one page or walking to the corner. When a goal is easy you will actually do it, and the doing teaches you that you are the sort of person who follows through, which is far more valuable than the goal itself. Once the habit is firmly established, the staircase can be made a little taller, one step at a time.

Goals that you can complete in a single day give you a small feeling of achievement every evening, like a coin dropped into a jar. A goal that takes a year to reach gives you that feeling only once, and rather late, with a long and discouraging wait in between. If you would like to travel far, it helps to arrange for a pleasant stop every night.

Each morning, Grace writes three tiny jobs in her notebook: water the plants, read ten pages of her book and walk to the postbox. By lunchtime she has usually finished all three, and she feels ridiculously, disproportionately pleased with herself, like a pupil who has been given a gold star. A day that has been marked with three ticks is very hard to call wasted.

Kofi's first tiny goal is almost embarrassingly modest: he will wash the dishes before he leaves for work each evening. It takes only five minutes, but coming home to a clean sink in the grey dawn makes the whole flat feel calmer, as if someone kind had tidied up while he was out. The kind person who did the tidying, he reflects with a small smile, was none other than himself.

When you do not feel like starting, begin with the smallest possible part of the task, so small that it seems almost silly. If you want to go for a walk, simply put on your shoes and tie one lace, and permit yourself to stop there if you wish. Very often the second lace follows, and then the door, and then the pavement, but the first step is the only one that you have to promise.

Try the five-minute rule, which means promising yourself that you may stop after five minutes if you really want to. Starting is almost always the hardest part of any job, and once you have begun, you will often find that you want to carry on, rather as a stuck bicycle runs easily once it is moving. If you do stop after five minutes, you have still won, because five minutes is more than nothing.

A big job can feel utterly impossible when you look at it all at once, like a mountain of laundry that seems to grow while you stare at it. Fold one shirt first, and the mountain loses a stone, and then another, until you find that you are halfway through without having made any grand decision. Overwhelm is a trick of the eyes, and the cure for it is to look at only one thing.

Gentle goals grow by inches rather than by miles, like stepping stones laid one at a time across a wide lawn. When this week's goal begins to feel easy, add a very small piece to it for the following week, and then keep adding patiently and without fuss. Slow growth is hardly noticeable from day to day, but it is astonishing when you look back over a year.

If you miss a day, that is not a failure but merely an ordinary day, and the chain of ticks can begin again tomorrow without a single word of reproach. What matters is not a perfect record, which hardly anyone achieves, but how kindly and how quickly you come back to the plan. A gap in a row of ticks is only a gap, and it says nothing at all about your character.

In the evening, Grace in her armchair and Kofi in his kitchen each look down at a list with a few ticks on it. Neither day was exciting, and neither of them would have thought it worth describing to a stranger, yet each of them feels quietly that the day was well spent. That feeling, repeated night after night, is what slowly turns a heavy life into a lighter one.

Being bored and having no purpose at all are quite different experiences, although they can feel alike on a wet afternoon. Boredom says, “I want something to do,” whereas a lack of purpose says, “Nothing is worth doing,” and noticing which of the two you are hearing is a useful first step. Boredom can be cured with a book or a walk, but the other feeling needs a gentler and longer kind of attention.

Boredom is an uncomfortable guest in any house, but it can also turn out to be a door. Every parent has watched a bored child suddenly invent an absorbing game with two spoons and a cardboard box, because the mind needs a little empty space before it begins to create. If we fill every spare minute with a screen, we give that creative restlessness nowhere to go.

Boredom is a hungry, restless feeling, and it longs for something interesting to do. A flat and heavy feeling that nothing matters is a different matter altogether, and if it lingers for weeks, it deserves much more careful attention than a new hobby can provide. Learning to tell the two apart is a kindness to yourself, because they call for different kinds of help.

Sometimes you are not short of reasons at all but merely short of sleep, and exhaustion can disguise itself very convincingly as despair. If you have been working hard or sleeping badly for a long time, rest first, and only then ask yourself again whether you have a reason to get up. Rest is not the enemy of purpose but its foundation, and nobody builds anything lasting while permanently exhausted.

After a punishing week of night shifts, Kofi sleeps for a full ten hours on Sunday, in a room as dark as a cave. When he wakes the world looks distinctly lighter, and he realises with some astonishment how much of his gloom had simply been exhaustion in a cheap disguise. It does not solve everything, but it makes the next problem a good deal smaller.

Slowing down to enjoy a small pleasure, such as a hot cup of tea on a wet afternoon, gives the day its taste. Most of us gulp the tea while looking at something else and then wonder where the day went, whereas a few minutes of real attention can make a single cup memorable. A pleasure that is never noticed might just as well never have happened, and it is a shame to waste so many.

Doing nothing on purpose, and without any guilt, is quite different from scrolling mindlessly while your thoughts slide away. Sit by the window with a warm mug and watch the rain run down the glass, and let your mind wander wherever it pleases, even into idle and slightly silly places. A rested mind often produces its best ideas at exactly the moments when nobody is demanding any of them.

One morning, Grace decides to eat a ripe pear with her full attention, noticing the sweet smell, the faint grain of the flesh and the juice running down her wrist. She realises that for years she had been eating without tasting, always doing something else at the same time, and that a pear is a small miracle if you let it be one. It cost her nothing at all, and yet it was easily the best moment of her whole day.

Kofi decides that Sunday afternoon, once the cooking is finished, will be set aside for resting, without apology or explanation. He lies in the park with his jacket folded under his head and his eyes closed, and he gradually stops feeling guilty about doing nothing at all. A rest that has been planned and permitted feels quite different from one that is stolen, and it works a good deal better.

Rest recharges the battery on which every reason runs, and without it even the best plan will eventually flicker and fade. Taking enough of it is not a break from your plan but an essential part of it, as necessary as the walking group or the tomato plant. Nobody expects a phone to work all day without charging, and yet we often expect it of ourselves.

Adults often forget how to play, because nearly everything we do has to be useful, healthy or productive in some way. Doing something purely for the fun of it, such as blowing bubbles in the park or kicking a ball against a wall, can give you back a surprising amount of energy. Play is not the opposite of seriousness but a different way of being alive.

Games played with other people, such as board games, cards or a deliberately silly quiz, make a cheerful reason to meet and a good excuse to stay a little longer. Nobody really minds who wins, and the laughter that bubbles up over a disputed rule is the real prize of the evening. Kofi and Yaw start a Wednesday card game, and it becomes a fixed point in a week that was lacking one.

In a shop on the high street, Grace buys a cheap box of watercolour paints and a pad of thick paper, and she carries them home like contraband. She cannot draw at all, and she knows it, but she badly wants to paint the birds that visit her window, and she has decided to try regardless. The wish to make something is itself a reason, and the result is almost beside the point.

Grace paints her first robin, and it looks distinctly like a tomato with legs and an air of mild surprise. She laughs until she has to wipe her eyes, pins it up on the kitchen wall anyway and finds that she enjoys looking at it far more than she expected to. Being bad at something is a surprisingly cheerful state once you have stopped caring about the verdict.

Being a beginner is perfectly fine, since everybody who has ever been good at anything once started without any skill at all. It may feel uncomfortable, especially for someone who is used to being competent, but it is exactly where every expert once stood. The embarrassment fades quickly, and the pleasure of improving lasts a great deal longer.

Grace joins a Wednesday evening class for beginners at the community centre, and she sits among a dozen strangers with her smudged paper and her borrowed brush. After forty years at the front of a classroom, she remembers with a jolt what it feels like to be the pupil, and she resolves to be a kinder teacher in her mind. The teacher is patient, and Grace finds that she can be patient with herself as well.

Kofi borrows an old guitar from Yaw, props a printed chord chart against a pillow and learns his first chord, which sounds appalling. His fingertips throb and the strings buzz, yet he grins like a child with a new toy, because for the first time in years he is doing something he cannot yet do. Difficulty, it turns out, is not the enemy of enjoyment when the stakes are low.

Wobbly pots, uneven stitches and wrong chords are all evidence that you have tried, and trying is precisely the point. A shelf of imperfect things is infinitely better than a shelf of perfect things that were never made, and every beginner's work holds a little of the person who made it. Perfectionism sounds like high standards, but in practice it very often just means never starting at all.

Children rarely mind being bad at things, because they are far too busy enjoying them to bother with the question of quality. We can borrow that attitude whenever we like, and we may well find that it fits better than the careful, self-critical one that we have been wearing for decades. Theo's wonky yellow sun on Grace's fridge is far more cheerful than any masterpiece.

After three weeks of stubborn practice, Kofi can play three chords and string them together into a tune that he actually recognises. It is far from beautiful, and Yaw has threatened to confiscate the guitar, but it is entirely his own, and he plays it twice in a row simply for the joy of hearing it. Progress of this kind, slow and clumsy and real, is among the best reasons to get up that exist.

Grace's neighbour Dev grows tomatoes in large pots on his patio, and he checks on them every morning before he does anything else. A living thing that depends on you gives the day a very gentle sort of structure, and the reward of a ripening fruit is one that you can taste. Even a single pot of herbs on a window sill can do the same.

Dev gives Grace a small pot, a bag of compost and a handful of tomato seeds, and he demonstrates exactly how deep to press them into the soil. She carries the pot home in both hands, as though it contained something far more precious than three seeds and a spoonful of earth. That evening she places it on the kitchen window sill and finds herself checking on it twice before bed.

On the sixth morning, a tiny green loop pushes its way through the surface of the soil, and Grace gasps aloud in her empty kitchen. Each day she bends to see whether the seedling has grown overnight, and each day, to her enormous satisfaction, it has, by an amount no bigger than a grain of rice. Nothing else in her life is changing so visibly, and nothing is quite so encouraging.

Grace now waters her seedling every morning with a small jug, and she finds herself getting up a little earlier simply to do it. Her mornings finally contain a job that genuinely needs her, and the plant does not mind in the least whether she is cheerful or glum. There is a great relief in being useful to something that asks no questions and makes no judgements.

Herbs such as basil, mint and parsley grow happily on a sunny window sill, even in the smallest of flats, and they forgive a great many mistakes. They are easy to look after and quick to reward you, because you can snip a few leaves into your supper on the very same day. It is a particular pleasure to eat something that you have personally kept alive, and the pleasure is hard to buy in a shop.

An animal that depends on you can give you a powerful reason to get up, since it must be fed, walked and talked to whatever the weather. A pet is a wonderful companion, but it is also a long commitment, and it is not right for everyone, so it deserves to be considered with care. The dog, of course, will have no doubts about the matter, and will be waiting at the door each morning with his lead.

Dev's sister owns a small, round dog called Biscuit who needs a walk on Monday afternoons, while she is at work, and Grace gladly volunteers to take him. Within a fortnight Biscuit is waiting at the garden gate with his lead in his mouth, quivering with joy, and Grace learns what it is to be the most important person in somebody's week. A dog's welcome, she reflects, is wonderfully uncomplicated, and it never depends on whether she has had a good day.

A pet is a big promise that may last for ten years or more, and it costs both money and time, so it deserves a great deal of thought before you commit. There are other ways to enjoy animals without owning one, such as walking a neighbour's dog, helping at a shelter or simply putting out seeds for the birds. The aim is to find a reason that lifts you, and not to acquire an obligation that you will secretly come to resent.

Kofi brings home a spider plant from the market, which Yaw assures him is almost impossible to kill, and he places it on the window sill beside the guitar. He waters it every Sunday after cooking, and he is secretly proud when it sends out a long stem with a tiny new plant dangling from the end. Looking after something small turns out to be good for the person doing the looking.

In late summer, Grace's tomato plant finally produces its first red fruit, and she cuts it into thick slices with great ceremony. She and Dev share it over the fence with a pinch of salt, and for a moment neither of them says anything, because there is nothing to add to a taste like that. The reward of caring for something over many weeks is sweeter than anything you could buy.

One quiet night, Kofi gathers his courage and asks his manager, Ms Okoro, whether he might learn how the warehouse stock system works. He expects a polite refusal, but she smiles broadly and says that she has been waiting for months for somebody to ask. Sometimes the door that we assume to be locked has simply never been tried by anyone.

Ms Okoro agrees to teach Kofi the stock system on quiet nights, for one hour at a time, and she proves to be a patient and rather funny teacher. The screens are bewildering at first, with their columns and codes, but little by little Kofi begins to see how the whole warehouse fits together like a large, logical puzzle. A good teacher, as Grace would say, makes the difficult feel possible, and Ms Okoro is plainly a good one.

While counting boxes on a high shelf, Kofi notices that an entire row has been given the wrong label, which would have caused a muddle by the morning. He corrects the record, and the little victory brightens the rest of his shift, as though someone had switched on a lamp in a corner he had not realised was dark. Work, he is finding, is much less dull when you understand what it is for.

Learning a genuine skill at work gives you a path to follow, and Kofi starts to see where his job might lead if he keeps going. By the end of the month he is given a small blue badge for the stock team, and he pins it to his vest with the carefulness of a soldier receiving a medal. The badge is only a scrap of plastic, but it tells him quietly that somebody has noticed his effort.

You may not be able to change your job, at least not this month, but you can often change the way in which you regard it. Hunt for something to learn, a colleague to assist or a small process to improve, and the same shelves and the same shifts begin to look different. A job that feels like a prison to one person can feel like a workshop to another.

Money is a genuine worry for a great many people, and nobody should pretend otherwise or suggest that cheerfulness can pay the rent. If you are struggling to meet your bills, a new hobby is not the answer, and it is sensible to look for practical help from an advice service or a trusted friend. Having said that, a lack of money does not have to mean a lack of reasons.

Many of the best reasons cost nothing whatever, since a sunset seen from a hilltop is entirely free and quite as splendid as anything that money can buy. A walk beside a river, a conversation with a friend and a morning among the trees are all within reach of any pocket, however empty. The most beautiful things in a day are usually the ones that nobody has thought to charge for.

Your local library will lend you books, music and often films without charging you a penny, and it is usually warm and welcoming into the bargain. Many libraries also run reading groups, talks and craft mornings that anyone can join, which makes them among the best-value reasons to leave the house. Grace, who has known this for sixty years, enjoys explaining it to anybody who will listen.

Make a list in your notebook of all the free pleasures that lie within walking distance of your home, and keep adding to it as you notice more. You might include a park, a street market, a museum with free entry, a hill with a good view and a bench that catches the afternoon sun. A list like this is a quiet reassurance that the world is richer than your bank account suggests.

One afternoon, Grace and Kofi both happen to stop at the noticeboard outside the bakery, and they begin to read the posters about free events together, murmuring their opinions. It is the first time that they have exchanged more than a greeting, and they are both surprised to find how easy the conversation is. Two people who have been nodding at each other for weeks finally discover what the other one is like.

Choose one thing to look forward to in each month of the coming year, and mark it with a small star on the calendar. They do not need to be grand, since a market, a film or a birthday lunch will serve, but together they turn a blank year into a path with landmarks along it. Months without a star are the ones in which the heaviest mornings tend to gather.

Grace puts a bright star on a Saturday in June, and she writes the single word “sea” beside it in her neatest handwriting. She has not been to the seaside in six years, and she finds herself imagining the sound of the waves and the taste of chips eaten on a cold bench. The day is still months away, but it has already begun to warm the rooms in between.

Kofi circles the date of Abena's birthday dinner in August with a fat red pen, and he decides on the spot that he will cook it himself. He intends to serve their gran's groundnut stew to the whole family, which means that he has five months in which to practise and perfect every step of the recipe. Having a date with a purpose attached to it turns his quiet Sundays into rehearsals for something that matters.

A wish is far more likely to come true once it has a date beside it, so do not leave your plans floating in the vague future. Circle the day on the calendar, tell a friend about it, and you will feel its pull growing stronger as it approaches. A date turns a hope into an appointment, and appointments are hard to ignore.

Each evening, write down three good things that happened during the day, however small they may seem. The habit trains your eyes to notice what went well, instead of letting your attention rush straight to what went wrong, as it tends to do. Over weeks, the little list becomes a private treasure that you can open on any difficult morning.

Some people keep their good things in a jar, with one folded note for each day, so that by the end of the year the jar is full. On a heavy morning, you can pull out a handful of notes and read them, and the reminder that good days really do happen can lift your mood a little. It is a small act of kindness to your future self, who will be grateful.

One evening, Grace's list reads that Dev gave her a tomato, that Theo sent her a drawing of a purple rabbit and that the sun came out just as she reached the park. She puts down her pen and realises how many small kindnesses she used to let slip past her unnoticed, like pebbles dropped through a hole in a pocket. The little list, written each night before bed, has slowly taught her how to hold on to them.

It is never too late to begin something new, whatever your age, whether it is a course, a language or a musical instrument. Many people have started such things in their seventies and eighties and have found enormous pleasure in them, though they are inclined to say that they wish they had begun sooner. The best moment to start is rarely the perfect one, but it is almost always the present.

Kofi shyly asks Grace whether she would be willing to look at a letter that he has written, applying for an evening course in stock control. She takes out her old red pen with a grin that makes her look thirty years younger, and over a pot of tea they turn his nervous sentences into clear and confident ones. Grace sees that she is still a teacher, even though her job has ended.

Kofi walks to the postbox at the end of the road and drops his letter through the slot before he has time to change his mind. Whether he is accepted or not, he is quietly proud of himself for having tried, and he walks home with a springier step than he has had in years. Taking a risk, even a modest one, reminds us that our lives are still open.

Some days you will fail to get out of bed, however good your plans may be, and it is important to know this in advance. That is not the end of the story, since a bad morning is an event rather than an identity, and you can begin again tomorrow without a speech of apology. Learning to restart gracefully is a far more valuable skill than the impossible one of never stopping.

After a week of relentless rain and a heavy cold, Grace stays in bed for three mornings in a row, with the curtains drawn and the bird book unopened. The old heaviness has returned like an unwelcome relative, and she feels as though all her careful progress has evaporated in a single damp week. It is a miserable feeling, and she does not try to argue herself out of it.

Grace imagines that a friend has come to her with exactly the same story, and she asks herself what she would say in reply. She would say, without hesitation, that it is all right to rest, that a cold is a good reason to stay in bed and that nothing is ruined, so she says precisely this to herself aloud. Most of us are far kinder to our friends than to ourselves, and the habit is worth reversing.

After a difficult week at the warehouse, Kofi slides back into his old habit of endless scrolling and loses an entire weekend to it. The old pattern is strong, because it is easy and always available, and on Monday he feels angry with himself and suspects that he has wasted all his effort. He has not; the skills he built are still there, only temporarily out of sight.

When you have slipped back, resist the temptation to launch a grand rescue plan, and take the smallest step you can think of instead. Open the curtain, drink a glass of water or put on your shoes, and let the next step follow when it is ready, without any pressure to hurry. Getting back onto a path that you have already walked is much easier than making a brand new one.

If you feel that nothing interests you for many weeks, or if your sleep, appetite and energy have changed a great deal, please speak to a doctor. Low mood is common and often treatable, and asking for help is a sensible act rather than a sign of weakness, since this book is general encouragement and cannot replace medical advice. You deserve proper support, and it is available, so please do not feel that you have to carry this quietly by yourself.

If you ever feel that life is not worth living, or that you might harm yourself, please tell someone at once, and do not wait for a better moment. Contact your local emergency number or a helpline in your country, where trained and patient people are ready to listen at any hour. A reason to get up is not something to find alone in a crisis, and asking for help is itself a brave and sensible act.

On a Saturday morning, Grace and Kofi sit side by side on a park bench with warm rolls from the bakery, watching the dogs argue over a stick. After a long and comfortable silence, Kofi admits that he finds the mornings extremely hard, and the words come out much more easily than he had expected. It is easier to say something difficult to a person who is looking at the view instead of at you.

Grace listens carefully, nods and then tells Kofi that she has found the mornings hard as well, and that she has done so for many months. He is visibly relieved to learn that he is not strange, and she is relieved to have said the words out loud, since neither of them had told anyone before. A trouble shared is not always halved, but it very often becomes far easier to carry.

Grace and Kofi agree to take a walk together every Saturday morning, finishing, naturally, at the bakery for warm bread and a cup of tea. Each of them now has a reason that depends on the other, and neither is willing to let the other down, which is a more reliable alarm than anything that ticks. It is the kind of friendship that might never have happened if either had stayed in bed.

A reason that works beautifully in spring may have faded by autumn, and that is no cause for alarm. Take your list out every few months, drop whatever has lost its pull, and add something fresh, much as a gardener alters what grows in each season. A life with a living list of reasons is more resilient than a life with a single, fixed one.

Mae invites Grace to give a short talk about garden birds at the library, and a dozen people come, including two of the Tuesday walkers and the boy in the green jumper. They ask her thoughtful, delightful questions, and she realises that she is still a teacher at heart, only now she teaches because she wants to rather than because a timetable demands it. Retirement ended her job, but it did not end the thing that she was good at.

When winter arrives, the outdoor reasons become harder to enjoy, so it is wise to look for warm ones indoors. A pot of soup on the stove, a good book and a glowing lamp can be every bit as inviting as a walk in the summer sunshine, and they are much easier to arrange on a dark afternoon. Planning for the hard season before it comes is a gentle form of self-respect.

An email arrives on a grey Tuesday, and Kofi reads it three times before he believes that he has been offered a place on the stock-control course. Ms Okoro rearranges his shifts so that he can attend on Thursday evenings, and he feels the odd mixture of nerves and pride that always comes with a new beginning. He texts Grace first, before he even tells Abena, and she replies with a row of exclamation marks.

Let us gather the main ideas of this book into one place before we part, like objects arranged on a shelf. Look for modest reasons rather than grand ones, share your days with other people who expect and enjoy you, and keep asking questions about the world around you. None of these things is especially difficult, and each of them makes the others easier.

Remember also to set goals that are gentle enough to meet, to rest without apology when you are tired, and to play now and then simply for the pleasure of it. When you slip, as everyone does, begin again with the smallest step you can find, and treat yourself the way that you would treat a friend. If the heaviness lasts for weeks, speak to a doctor, because help is real and it works for many people.

Your list will not look like Grace's, or like Kofi's, and it should not, because a reason is an intensely personal thing. Some people are moved by birds, some by stew, some by a Tuesday walk or a Saturday match, and the best reason of all is whichever one makes you want to put your feet on the floor. Nobody else can choose it for you, but anybody can help you find it.

A year on, Grace still drinks her morning tea on the front step at dawn, and Kofi still walks past on his way home from the night shift, carrying warm bread from the bakery. He hands her a roll, sits down on the step beside her, and they watch the street waking up, while Dev waters his tomatoes and waves with the hose. Nothing about the scene is remarkable, and yet both of them know how far they have come to reach it.

Tonight, before you turn out the light, open your notebook and write down one small reason to get up tomorrow, using plain and honest words. It might be a cup of tea, a message to an old friend or a walk to the corner and back, and nobody else need ever see it. The act of writing it down is a small promise that you are making to the person you will be in the morning.

Tomorrow morning, in two houses not far apart, a retired teacher and a night-shift worker will each pull back a curtain as the sun comes up, and in a third house, perhaps, so will you. The alarm will ring exactly as it always has, but this time there will be something on the other side of it that is waiting for you. That, quietly and without any fuss, is how nearly every good day begins, and tomorrow's can begin that way for you.
